articles.title: This is Big Tech’s playbook for swallowing the AI industry
articles.summary: Amazon has replicated an antitrust-avoidance playbook pioneered by Microsoft with its hiring of most of the team behind buzzy AI startup Adept.
articles.body: A couple of months ago, I was sitting in the audience at a tech conference in San Fransisco watching Bloomberg’s Emily Chang interview Reid Hoffman. She asked about Microsoft’s hiring of the team behind Inflection, a would-be OpenAI competitor that Hoffman co-founded. It was an acquisition in everything but name, clearly designed to avoid the scrutiny of antitrust regulators. Not only had Microsoft (where Hoffman is a board member) hired most of Inflection’s employees — it also licensed the startup’s technology in a way that seemed designed to make its investors whole. Speaking with Chang that day onstage, Hoffman predicted that what happened to Inflection will become a “pattern” for future AI deals. We are seeing that pattern play out now. Last Friday, Amazon announced that it is hiring most of the team behind Adept, another would-be OpenAI competitor that raised about $400 million from top-tier investors to build, in the words of CEO David Luan, “a new type of giant model that turns natural language into actions on your machine.” Alexandra Miller, an Amazon spokesperson, told The Verge that the company had hired “close to” to 66 percent of Adept’s employees. In an internal memo published by GeekWire’s Taylor Soper, SVP Rohit Prasad said that, like Microsoft with Inflection, Amazon will also be licensing Adept’s technology to “accelerate our roadmap for building digital agents that can automate software workflows.” Adept’s corporate blog post about the news suggests it was running out of money: “Continuing with Adept’s initial plan of building both useful general intelligence and an enterprise agent product would’ve required spending significant attention on fundraising for our foundation models, rather than bringing to life our agent vision.” Recent reports say the company has been looking to sell itself. The reality is that building leading AI models is extremely costly, and raising $400 million isn’t even enough to compete these days. Big Tech, meanwhile, is flush with cash and looking to get in on what everyone perceives to be the next big thing. It’s logical for more AI startups to go the way of Inflection and Adept as the industry consolidates. The problem for Big Tech is that they are no longer allowed to buy companies like they once did. The current antitrust enforcement regime would most certainly try to block an Amazon acquisition of Adept, whether there is a strong legal argument for doing so or not. (Amazon execs are still seething about not being allowed to buy a robot vacuum cleaner company.) Even still, capitalism finds a way. What Microsoft did to Inflection, and what Amazon just did to Adept, is the new Big Tech playbook for swallowing the AI industry and getting away with it. Silicon Valley has a storied history of acquihires, where a startup is gutted for its people and left for dead. Microsoft and Amazon have done what are essentially reverse acquihires, where the hiring of people and a corresponding licensing deal is designed to disguise what is actually an acquisition. Reid Hoffman, meanwhile, should probably be congratulated for more than just an accurate prediction about the future of these deals — one of Adept’s earliest investors was none other than his venture capital firm, Greylock. Correction, July 1st: A previous version of this story incorrectly stated the percentage of Adept employees hired by Amazon. The percentage is “close to” 66 percent, not 80 percent.

articles.title: Thomson Reuters wins an early court battle over AI, copyright, and fair use
articles.summary: A judge ruled in favor of Thomson Reuters in its Westlaw copyright infringement lawsuit against Ross Intelligence, an AI startup.
articles.body: On Tuesday, US District Court of Delaware judge Stephanos Bibas issued a partial summary judgment in favor of Thomson Reuters in its copyright infringement lawsuit against Ross Intelligence, a legal AI startup. Filed in 2020, it’s one of the first cases that will deal with the legality of AI tools and how they are trained, often using copyrighted data scraped from somewhere else without license or permission. Similar lawsuits against OpenAI, Microsoft, and other AI giants are currently winding their way through the courts, and they could come down to similar questions about whether or not the AI tools can claim a “fair use” defense of using copyrighted material. In a statement given to The Verge by Thomson Reuters spokesperson Jeff McCoy, the company said: > We are pleased that the court granted summary judgment in our favor and concluded that Westlaw’s editorial content created and maintained by our attorney editors, is protected by copyright and cannot be used without our consent. The copying of our content was not “fair use.” However, as the judge noted, this case involved “non-generative” AI, not a generative AI tool like an LLM. Ross shut down in 2021, calling the lawsuit “spurious” but saying it was unable to raise enough funding to keep going while caught up in a legal battle. As reported previously by Wired, today Judge Bibas wrote in his decision, “None of Ross’s possible defenses holds water” against accusations of copyright infringement, and ultimately rejected Ross’s fair-use defense, relying heavily on the factor of how Ross’s use of copyrighted material affected the market for the original work’s value by building a direct competitor. Thomson Reuters sued over Ross’s use of its Westlaw search engine. Westlaw indexes a good deal of material that is not copyrightable (like legal decisions) but also intersperses it with its own content. For instance, Westlaw headnotes — which are summaries of points of law written by human editors — are a signature feature meant to make the very expensive Westlaw subscription attractive to lawyers. In building a legal research search engine, Ross turned the annotations and headnotes “into numerical data about the relationships among legal words to feed into its AI,” wrote Bibas. The ruling describes how, after Thomson Reuters rejected its attempt to license Westlaw’s content, Ross turned to another company, LegalEase, and purchased 25,000 Bulk Memos of questions and answers written by lawyers using the Westlaw headnotes that it used for training data. Ross CEO Andrew Arruda claimed the Westlaw data was “added noise” and that its tool “aims to recognize and extract answers directly from the law using machine learning.” However, after having “compared how similar each of the 2,830 Bulk Memo questions, headnotes, and judicial opinions are, one by one,” the judge said the evidence of actual copying was “so obvious that no reasonable jury could find otherwise.”

articles.title: Cavalos voltam a ser reconhecidos como seres que sentem emoções em SC | G1
articles.standfirst: Decisão unânime do Tribunal de Justiça de Santa Catarina derrubou lei de 2018 que havia retirado os cavalos da lista de animais reconhecidos como seres sencientes.
articles.summary: Decisão unânime do Tribunal de Justiça de Santa Catarina derrubou lei de 2018 que havia retirado os cavalos da lista de animais reconhecidos como seres sencientes.
articles.body:
Cavalos voltam a ser reconhecidos como seres capazes de sentir emoções em SC; entenda — Foto: Divulgação

A Justiça de Santa Catarina restabeleceu o reconhecimento dos cavalos como seres sencientes e sujeitos de direito no estado.

A decisão unânime do Tribunal de Justiça de Santa Catarina (TJSC), publicada na terça-feira (13), declarou inconstitucional uma lei estadual de 2018 que havia retirado os equinos dessa classificação no Código Estadual de Proteção aos Animais.

🐴 Animais "sencientes" são aqueles capazes de sentir e perceber o mundo de forma consciente. Isso significa que os cavalos não apenas reagem a estímulos, mas vivenciam sensações e emoções como dor, medo, alegria e afeto.

Em janeiro de 2018, a lei estadual 17.485 passou a reconhecer cães, gatos e cavalos como seres sencientes e sujeitos de direito em Santa Catarina.

Meses depois, a lei estadual 17.526 retirou os cavalos dessa lista, mantendo apenas cães e gatos no texto.

O Ministério Público de Santa Catarina (MPSC) questionou a mudança na Justiça. Para o órgão, a retirada dos cavalos representou um retrocesso na proteção dos animais, já que eles deixaram de ter esse reconhecimento expresso na legislação estadual.

O desembargador Jairo Fernandes Gonçalves, relator do processo, entendeu que a mudança reduziu a proteção anteriormente garantida aos equinos.

A decisão foi acompanhada por unanimidade pelos demais integrantes do Órgão Especial do TJSC.

A Justiça também considerou que o interesse em evitar possíveis impactos do reconhecimento dos cavalos sobre atividades econômicas e esportivas não era justificativa suficiente para diminuir a proteção prevista na lei.

Cavalos voltam a ser reconhecidos como seres capazes de sentir emoções em SC — Foto: Divulgação

Com a decisão, volta a valer o texto anterior da legislação estadual, que reconhece cães, gatos e cavalos como seres sencientes e sujeitos de direito .

Na prática, os cavalos voltam a aparecer expressamente na lei catarinense nessa condição. A decisão também tem efeito retroativo, ou seja, a lei que retirou esse reconhecimento deixa de valer desde que foi criada.

Para o procurador de Justiça Isaac Newton Belota Sabba Guimarães, coordenador do Centro de Apoio Operacional do Controle de Constitucionalidade do MPSC, a decisão acompanha os avanços na proteção dos animais e reforça a necessidade de evitar maus-tratos e sofrimento físico indevido.

"Ao restabelecer o reconhecimento expresso dos cavalos como seres sencientes e sujeitos de direito, o Tribunal prestigia a evolução da legislação e o compromisso da sociedade com a proteção integral dos animais", destacou o procurador.

articles.title: Detran-PR anuncia concurso público com 100 vagas | G1
articles.standfirst: Será o primeiro concurso para o órgão em 20 anos, conforme o Governo do Paraná.
articles.summary: Será o primeiro concurso para o órgão em 20 anos, conforme o Governo do Paraná.
articles.body:
O Detran-PR anunciou um concurso público com 100 vagas para contratar Agentes e Analistas de Trânsito. Será o primeiro concurso para o órgão em 20 anos, conforme o Governo do Paraná.

A portaria que estabelece as regiões de concorrência, a distribuição das vagas e a abrangência territorial do concurso foi publicada nesta sexta-feira (16).

Ela detalha a divisão territorial das vagas destinadas ao cargo de Agente de Trânsito. São 25 vagas para Curitiba e Região Metropolitana e 69 para o Interior do estado.

As outras seis vagas são para cargos administrativos (administrador, contador, economista, engenheiro civil, médico e psicólogo) na Sede Administrativa do Detran-PR, em Curitiba.

O edital do concurso será elaborado em conjunto com a Fundaseg e deve ser publicado nos próximos meses. A contratação da banca e a publicação do edital serão feitas pela fundação.

Segundo a portaria, as vagas adicionais que eventualmente venham a ser autorizadas durante o prazo de validade do concurso público, que deve ser de dois anos, poderão ser distribuídas entre as regiões de concorrência mediante ato próprio da autarquia.

Segundo o governo, de maneira geral, o Agente de Trânsito desempenha atividades técnicas, administrativas, operacionais e fiscalizatórias relacionadas às competências legais do Detran-PR, nos termos do Código de Trânsito Brasileiro.

Além disso, tem como função analisar, instruir, acompanhar, fiscalizar e subsidiar processos administrativos relacionados à habilitação de condutores, registro e licenciamento de veículos, infrações, penalidades, entidades credenciadas, identificação veicular, segurança viária, sinalização, educação para o trânsito e demais áreas de atuação do Detran-PR.

Conforme o Governo do Paraná, está na fase final de aprovação o Perfil Profissiográfico do cargo de Agente de Trânsito, que vai embasar o edital do concurso público. Ele prevê que o cargo exija ensino médio completo e Carteira Nacional de Habilitação , categoria B ou superior, em situação regular.

articles.title: Estudantes denunciam deputado e ex-candidata por rasgarem panfletos na UFRR: 'Insegurança' | G1
articles.standfirst: Os alunos de Direito denunciaram ao Ministério Público Federal o deputado estadual Marcinho Belota (PL) e a ex-candidata a deputada federal Athally Albuquerque (Republicanos).
articles.summary: Os alunos de Direito denunciaram ao Ministério Público Federal o deputado estadual Marcinho Belota (PL) e a ex-candidata a deputada federal Athally Albuquerque (Republicanos).
articles.body:
Ação aconteceu no bloco de Direito da Universidade Federal de Roraima — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Os estudantes do curso de Direito da Universidade Federal de Roraima (UFRR) denunciaram o deputado estadual Marcinho Belota (PL) e da ex-candidata da deputada federal Athally Albuquerque (Republicanos). A denúncia feita ao Ministério Público Federal (MPF) aponta que eles destruíram panfletos informativos no campus universitário nesta sexta-feira (16) em Boa Vista .

De acordo com a denúncia, os dois entraram na instituição alegando que os panfletos com informações sobre o presidenciável Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) eram "fake news" . Antes da ação, eles teriam procurado a Reitoria da UFRR para pedir a retirada do material, mas o pedido foi negado porque a universidade entendeu que a divulgação respeitava a legislação eleitoral.

O g1 entrou em contato com a assessoria de Marcinho Belota e de Athally Albuquerque, mas até a última atualização da reportagem não houve resposta.

Ainda conforme o registro da denúncia, os dois foram até o bloco do curso e rasgaram os materiais deixados pelos estudantes. O documento também afirma que eles tentaram provocar os alunos presentes para gerar confronto . A ação foi registrada em vídeo.

Os estudantes alegam que a conduta configura crime eleitoral por inutilização de propaganda regularmente afixada.

"A regularidade da propaganda foi atestada pela autoridade administrativa competente da universidade, e a eventual discordância dos noticiados deveria ter sido levada à Justiça Eleitoral pela via própria (art. 96 da Lei nº 9.504/1997), e não resolvida por meio da destruição do material pelas próprias mãos", cita trecho da denúncia.

Segundo a denúncia, o principal enquadramento é o crime previsto no artigo 331 do Código Eleitoral, que trata da inutilização, alteração ou perturbação de propaganda eleitoral devidamente empregada . Subsidiariamente, a representação aponta possível enquadramento no artigo 332 do mesmo código, que prevê punição para quem impedir ou embaraçar a propaganda eleitoral.

Amanda Almeida, aluna do curso de Direito do 10º semestre, contou que os materiais foram financiados pelos próprios alunos e ex-alunos , sem participação de partidos políticos .

"Nós pegamos notícias com links reais, fizemos panfletos para a gente poder panfletar em eventos políticos na cidade, fizemos bótons, fizemos adesivos e uma bandeira e os dizeres eram simplesmente ' Direito UFRR Antifascista'. Não havia manifestação político-partidária", contou.

Após a destruição dos panfletos, o movimento estudantil arrecadou quase R$ 6 mil em doações e pretende imprimir mais materiais para continuar a distribuição. Por outro lado, Amanda conta que, após a ação do deputado estadual e da ex-candidata o sentimento é de medo .

"A gente está se sentindo inseguro para voltar para dentro da nossa própria faculdade. A gente quer se formar. Eu tenho que me formar esse ano. Como é que eu vou voltar para a faculdade na segunda-feira", contou.

Em nota divulgada neste sábado (17), a UFRR manifestou "veemente repúdio" aos atos de invasão e depredação ocorridos no Centro Acadêmico de Direito. A instituição afirmou que divergências políticas fazem parte da vida universitária, mas destacou que não tolerará intimidação, destruição de patrimônio ou ações que comprometam o ambiente democrático.

A universidade informou ainda que adotará medidas administrativas, legais e judiciais para apurar os fatos e responsabilizar os envolvidos.

"Divergências de pensamentos, posicionamentos políticos ou ideológicos fazem parte da vida acadêmica de uma instituição que respeita a democracia. O que não pode ser admitido, sob qualquer justificativa, é que essas divergências se transformem em invasão de espaços, intimidação, destruição de bens, ou qualquer forma de violência ou desrespeito", afirmou em nota.

O Centro Acadêmico da UFRR pede que o MPF investigue o caso e adote as providências cabíveis. A representação foi protocolada na Procuradoria da República em Roraima.

articles.title: Peter Schiff warns a ‘perfect storm of financial destruction’ worse than 2008 is brewing. Build wealth beyond your home
articles.summary: Schiff estimates $2 trillion in paper losses on low-rate mortgages — here's what it means for your wealth.
articles.body:

The low mortgage rate you locked in years ago might be one of your best financial decisions. Peter Schiff argued it could also be part of a "perfect storm of financial destruction that is about to hit."

"Mortgage lenders will lose far more during the developing mortgage crisis than they did during all of the GFC," Schiff warned in an Oct. 15 post on X (1), referring to the global financial crisis.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Priority Gold's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

He claimed, "Even without a single default, on paper mortgage lenders have already lost over four times more than they lost during the GFC."

He blamed the Federal Reserve's prolonged low interest rates and government-backed mortgages that let borrowers lock in cheap financing for decades.

An alarming forecast, especially if your home represents much of your wealth or you're counting on your investments to carry you through retirement.

But before you start picturing another foreclosure crisis, there's an important distinction: A mortgage losing value to an investor doesn't automatically mean your house has lost value, your payment is going up, or your lender is about to fail.

And keep in mind, if your loan or its servicing changes hands, the new company can't just rewrite your agreement (2).

Why Schiff sees trouble in low-rate mortgages

"There is currently about $8.3 trillion in outstanding fixed-rate mortgages with an average rate of 4.6% and 25 years left to maturity," Schiff wrote. "Given that current rates are 7.5%, the mark-to-market losses on those mortgages are already about $2 trillion. When rates rise to 8.5%, the loss will rise to $3 trillion!"

For comparison, Schiff put realized losses on defaulted mortgages during 2007–2010 at about $450 billion.

Keep in mind these are Schiff's estimates, and his 8.5% scenario isn't today's reality. The latest Freddie Mac survey (3), released Oct. 15, put the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 7.40%, up from 6.27% a year earlier.

Here's the basic pricing problem: If a new mortgage pays a substantially higher rate, an investor generally won't pay full price for an otherwise comparable older loan paying much less. The older loan then needs a discount to compete.

articles.title: US Interest Costs Hit Record $1 Trillion, Risking Debt Snowball
articles.summary: The US government’s debt interest burden reached a record high for fiscal 2026, eating up a growing share of federal revenue and risking a snowballing of bor...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The US government's debt interest burden reached a record high for fiscal 2026, eating up a growing share of federal revenue and risking a snowballing of borrowing that could leave the country more vulnerable to economic shocks.

For the year through September, net interest costs came to $1.05 trillion, up more than 8% from the $970 billion in fiscal 2025, Treasury Department data showed Friday. The Peter G. Peterson Foundation, a research group, sees the costs reaching 3.2% of gross domestic product, surpassing the previous record, reached in 1991. GDP figures for last quarter are due later this month.

The increase reflects both that there's a lot more debt to pay interest on — one key measure exceeds $32 trillion, some $10 trillion more than just five years ago — but also much higher interest rates. The average rate the government paid on marketable Treasuries was 3.52% at the end of September, more than double the 1.47% five years before.

What's worse is that current yields are even higher, with the current gauge from Bloomberg's US Treasuries index now around 5%. The rise in rates has prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent into extraordinary steps to contain the move, though economists argue the nation remains distant from crisis. Demand at debt auctions has proved solid, and higher borrowing costs aren't hindering credit flows.

"It doesn't seem like a crisis — it's kind of a slow eating away" of fiscal capacity, said Louise Sheiner, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and former economist at the Federal Reserve. What's unknown is the point at which "some lenders are going to decide not to lend to us — and if that happens, that could lead to a fiscal crisis," with the Treasury losing access to raise money from markets, she said.

Gennadiy Goldberg, head of US interest rates strategy at TD Securities, said one thing staving off deeper concerns for now is that the nation's nominal GDP growth rate — which is key for things like corporate revenues and tax receipts — is higher than US Treasury yields. The nominal year-on-year GDP gain for the second quarter was 6.3%. "A fiscal apocalypse is not upon us just yet," Goldberg wrote in a recent note.

articles.title: Elon Musk settles lawsuits over $1 million voter giveaway
articles.summary: Plaintiffs claiming Musk’s $1 million voter lottery was a fraud are settling for an undisclosed sum.
articles.body: In 2024, Elon Musk promised to give away $1 million a day to a randomly selected registered voter in a swing state. That prompted legal challenges, raised questions about its legality, and drew lawsuits from two Arizona residents claiming the lottery was a fraud. Musk has now agreed to settle the two lawsuits filed in Austin, Texas, though the details of the settlement have not been made public. The plaintiffs claim that when Musk announced the sweepstakes, he falsely claimed the prizes would be awarded randomly. Philadelphia’s District Attorney sued to stop the giveaway, claiming that Musk was running an illegal lottery. During a hearing, Chris Gober, a representative for Musk’s America PAC, told the judge that “The $1 million recipients are not chosen by chance … We know exactly who will be announced as the $1 million recipient today and tomorrow.” That directly contradicted Musk’s claim that the drawings were random. The plaintiffs say they never would have signed the petition required to enter the giveaway if they had known it wasn’t random. They accused Musk and America PAC of using it as a ploy to obtain user data and said the petition “places no limitations on America PAC’s use of or sale of the personal data it collects, nor does it provide any additional information about the planned use of data.”

articles.title: TikTok bans Musk documentary account
articles.summary: Larry Ellison’s TikTok has shut down the promotional account for Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary.
articles.body: Just ahead of the wider release of Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, TikTok has banned the film’s social media account from its platform. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, was informed Friday afternoon that a “permanent suspension” was imminent. Bleecker Street has not yet responded to a request for comment from The Verge. While TikTok has no official affiliation with Elon Musk, part owner Larry Ellison appears in the film via a text message offering to help Musk fund his Twitter purchase. Last month, YouTube, Meta, X, and TikTok all faced backlash for rejecting ads for the film. YouTube and Google quickly reversed course, calling it an “error.” However, TikTok and X have refused to change their stance, and neither platform has allowed paid advertisements for the film. Banning the documentary’s account, however, marks a serious escalation, and one laced with a dash of irony — shortly before the account was removed, it posted that people should see the movie “before it gets shut down.” [Image: The irony.

articles.title: TikTok permanently bans ‘Musk’ documentary advertising account
articles.summary: A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms.
articles.body:
A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms, with TikTok banning the film’s advertising account.

According to a story in The Hollywood Reporter , the documentary’s distributor Bleecker Street was recently notified by TikTok that the account had received a “permanent suspension” due to its political content. TechCrunch has reached out to TikTok for comment.

Ads promoting the trailer for “Musk” — directed by Oscar-winner filmmaker Alex Gibney — were initially rejected by Meta and YouTube as well , though those platforms eventually allowed the ad, with Meta blaming the rejection on “an error.” Gibney recently confirmed that the film’s international distributor Universal had wavered in its plans to release “Musk,” though it’s now moving forward.

X, which Musk owns, has refused to carry ads for “Musk.” TikTok’s U.S. operations are partly owned by Larry Ellison — who, like Musk, has been a notable supporter of President Donald Trump.

“Musk” opened in just four theaters last weekend and is now rolling out more broadly. Next year, it’s supposed to stream on HBO — now part of Paramount/Skydance and led by Ellison’s son David .

articles.title: ‘France, truly, is on the brink’ and just days away from a make-or-break moment in its debt crisis, analyst warns, as protests turn into riots
articles.summary: "France could be forced to seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund and to pray for it from the European Central Bank — a humiliation for the wor...
articles.body:
Nationwide protests over the high cost of living roiled France on Saturday, adding to turmoil over public spending and debt ahead of a critical vote in the National Assembly.

Rioting broke out in some cities as luxury boutiques and supermarkets were looted while public buildings were defaced and even set on fire.

That followed mass demonstrations earlier this month, with students decrying run-down classrooms, missing teachers, and buildings that aren't equipped for rising temperatures. Protestors blamed years of underinvestment in public education.

At the same time, France's looming debt has sent bond yields to the highest levels in 24 years, flashing warning signs not seen since the eurozone debt crisis in 2011.

With far-right and far-left candidates in the lead to become France's next president in the spring, markets are losing confidence that either side will take the painful steps necessary to rein in the deficit.

For Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at Eurasia Group, France is suffering from a crisis of liberal democracy, a crisis of fiscal mismanagement, and a crisis of youth disaffection.

"But the fiscal crisis is the most dangerous, underlying many of the country's woes and threatening to bring it to ruin," he wrote in a New York Times op-ed on Thursday. "France, truly, is on the brink."

The crises are also related to each other. For instance, Rahman pointed out that while France's education spending tops the European Union average, more than a quarter of the money pays for pensions of retired teachers.

Nobel laureate Paul Krugman similarly drew a straight line from France's retirement largesse to the student unrest. Due to its very generous government pension plan, education spending has suffered, meaning France is effectively subsidizing older French at the expense of everyone else, he wrote in a Substack post last week.

France's public debt is now a record $4 trillion, or 119% of GDP—the highest ratio since the immediate aftermath of World War II.

While the pandemic as well as the Ukraine and Iran wars worsened France's fiscal picture, President Emmanuel Macron has also pulled back from reforms meant to rein in the debt.

Sébastien Lecornu, the latest in a revolving door of prime ministers, has proposed a 2027 budget that would modestly bring the deficit down to 5% of GDP from 5.4%, and faces a first critical vote in the National Assembly on Tuesday.

"If his government fails to pass the budget, the cost of servicing French debt may explode," Rahman predicted. "France could be forced to seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund and to pray for it from the European Central Bank — a humiliation for the world's seventh-biggest economy."

articles.standfirst: Senador eleito com quase cinco milhões de votos falou à TV Integração sobre rodovias, dívidas do estado, segurança pública e outros temas em discussão no Congresso Nacional
articles.summary: Senador eleito com quase cinco milhões de votos falou à TV Integração sobre rodovias, dívidas do estado, segurança pública e outros temas em discussão no Congresso Nacional
articles.body:
Mais votado entre os mineiros, o senador eleito Domingos Sávio (PL) , atualmente deputado federal, recebeu quase cinco milhões de votos, 24,21% dos eleitores do estado. Domingos é natural de São Tiago , no Campo das Vertentes de Minas, e fez carreira política em Divinópolis , no Centro-Oeste.

Em entrevista à TV Integração, o senador eleito falou sobre as prioridades para o mandato no Senado e destacou a dívida de Minas e as condições das rodovias do estado, também defendeu mudanças no judiciário e na segurança pública.

Minas tem uma dívida de quase R$188 bilhões com a União, segundo dados mais recentes da Secretaria de Estado de Fazenda, acumulada ao longo dos anos. No fim do ano de 2025, o estado aderiu ao Programa de Pleno Pagamento de Dívidas dos Estados (Propag), da União, que oferece renegociação de débitos com o governo brasileiro.

Sancionada em maio de 2026, a lei 25.871/2026 autoriza o Governo de Minas Gerais a transferir ou vender 191 imóveis estaduais para a União com o objetivo de amortizar a dívida do Estado no âmbito do Propag. A União precisa receber formalmente os imóveis. Entre eles, estão: o Expominas (Belo Horizonte e São João del Rei), o Minascentro, o Automóvel Clube de Belo Horizonte, o Grande Hotel de Araxá e o Espaço do Conhecimento UFMG.

Domingos Sávio afirmou que é preciso rever o pagamento da dívida, para que ele "se volte para Minas sob a forma de investimento, de maneira automática", explicou.

O senador eleito defendeu, também, uma revisão da lista de ativos utilizados para amortizar parte da dívida: "foi feita uma lista enorme, nós queremos ter um cuidado grande para que aquilo que seja essencial para o povo mineiro seja preservado", afirmou.

Minas Gerais tem a pior segurança rodoviária do Sudeste e baixa proteção em 3 a cada 10 km de estrada , como apontou o estudo "rodovias que perdoam" da Confederação Nacional do Transporte (CNT). Para a CNT, além da quantidade de acidentes e das vidas perdidas nas rodovias, a falta de investimento gera impacto financeiro. No estado, apenas 22% das rodovias têm alto índice de segurança e 47% têm nível intermediário. O estudo foi embasado na qualidade precária do asfalto, ausência de acostamento, sinalização deficiente e falta de barreiras de proteção.

O senador eleito afirmou que, com a reversão de pagamentos ao Propag e com outras ações no Congresso, pretende garantir dinheiro, dentro do Departamento Nacional de Infraestrutura de Transportes (DNIT), para melhorias nas rodovias: "principalmente fazendo a duplicação em trechos de rodovias federais, que são um corredor da morte, em que a gente está pagando pedágio", completou.

Domingos também falou sobre as rodovias vicinais, aquelas em zonas rurais que, na maioria dos casos, não tem pavimentação asfáltica: "E o produtor rural? Como ir de uma cidade para a outra? Nós temos muitos trechos que são de 'estrada de chão' e a situação vira um pesadelo", afirmou.

Domingos Sávio (PL) defendeu, em entrevista, mudanças no Poder Judiciário brasileiro. Questionado sobre como promover mudanças sem enfraquecer a democracia e as garantias constitucionais, o senador eleito afirmou que a regra prevista na Constituição permite que uma reforma seja feita com base no voto da ampla maioria.

"O que enfraquece a democracia é quando ela é desrespeitada, quando a Constituição é desrespeitada, e eu sinto que ela está sendo desrespeitada hoje (…) Então é preciso não apenas que você seja capaz de usar os artigos que a Constituição já tem, como, é claro, ter a grandeza de verificar aquilo que precisa de ser aprimorado e aprimorar dentro da regra constitucional", defendeu.

O senador eleito também defendeu mudanças na segurança pública, disse que é necessário considerar as facções criminosas como organizações terroristas e ter a colaboração de outros países para combater esses criminosos, para ele isso não coloca em risco a soberania nacional.

“A única coisa que ocorre é que você pode ter a colaboração de outros países para enfrentar essa organização terrorista, que é o crime organizado, que hoje tem tentáculos em vários países”.

Em junho deste ano, os Estados Unidos passaram a classificar oficialmente o Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) e o Comando Vermelho (CV) como Organizações Terroristas Estrangeiras.

Sávio também afirmou que pretende promover a tramitação de um Projeto de Lei de autoria própria, que endurece as regras, no Código de Processo Penal, contra criminosos reincidentes. "O indivíduo é preso porque estava roubando celular ou porque invadiu uma residência, roubou alguma coisa, foi pego com o fruto do crime e vai na delegacia. E ali, depois da audiência de custódia, é solto, porque a legislação não prevê prisão preventiva para o reincidente (…) eu incluo no Código de Processo Penal um parágrafo dizendo que o reincidente ficará preso até a conclusão do seu processo. Acaba com esse negócio de prende solta", afirmou.

Domingos Sávio Campos Resende é natural de São Tiago no Campo das Vertentes de Minas, formou-se em Medicina Veterinária pela Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (UFMG) em 1983 e fez carreira política em Divinópolis no Centro-Oeste mineiro. Foi vereador entre 1993 e 1996 e prefeito entre 1997 e 2001.

Assumiu o cargo de deputado estadual na Assembleia Legislativa de Minas Gerais (ALMG), onde exerceu a função de 2003 a 2011 por dois mandatos, até migrar para a Câmara dos Deputados em Brasília, onde atuou como deputado federal por quatro mandatos consecutivos.

Este ano, pelo Partido Liberal (PL), foi eleito senador, com o maior número de votos em Minas Gerais, para os próximos oito anos.

Domingos Sávio tem atuação ligada ao agronegócio e aos produtores rurais. O deputado presidiu a Cooperativa Agropecuária de Divinópolis e a Cooperativa de Crédito Rural, além do Sindicato Rural da cidade. Também atuou na fundação de sistemas de cooperativismo de crédito no estado.

articles.title: CDC sends a ‘disease detective’ to Pennsylvania amid measles outbreak
articles.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is sending a disease expert to assist with the response to the ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania. “CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” the spokesperson told NBC News. The…
articles.body:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is sending a disease expert to assist with the response to the ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania.

“CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” the spokesperson told NBC News.

The Hill has reached out to the CDC for comment.

Pennsylvania has seen a surge in measles cases in recent months, reporting its sixth death from the disease last week. The Commonwealth surpassed 1,000 measles cases in early October.

The measles outbreak in the state has been the source of disagreement between state and federal officials. Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-Pa.) blamed the Trump administration for its rhetoric on vaccines and medicine, specifically Robert F. Kennedy Jr., secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS).

Shapiro and Kennedy, perhaps the most prominent vaccine skeptic in the U.S., clashed in August, with the governor claiming Kennedy is focused on conspiracy theories instead of providing assistance to Pennsylvania.

“I told him what would be most helpful is if he would join me in encouraging people to get vaccinated and stop spreading misinformation. He then launched into a tirade — talking about fetal tissue and blaming the previous Administration for this problem,” Shapiro wrote in a post to the social platform X. “He even told me it would be better if we went back to “natural measles.”

Kennedy claimed Shapiro provided no evidence that he’s spread the vaccine misinformation.

“During our phone conversation, Governor Shapiro also accused me of promoting vaccine misinformation. When I asked him for an example, he was unable to provide one,” Kennedy wrote on X at the time.

In that same post, Kennedy claimed at length that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine contained “fetal tissue,” an assertion which Shapiro and medical professionals reject. The American Academy of Pediatrics has said that vaccines do not contain fetal cells.

The MMR vaccination rate in Pennsylvania has declined in recent years, and less than 1 percent of measles cases in Pennsylvania are among vaccinated people, according to the Commonwealth’s health department.

President Trump signed an executive order in August recommending splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate shots, linking the vaccine to autism and at one point saying it was “lethal.” Experts have debunked links between the MMR vaccine and autism.

The CDC spokesperson told NBC News that CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz recommends the MMR vaccine as “the most effective” way to prevent infection.

articles.title: Trump's policies raised costs for all but the top 1%, report says
articles.summary: Trump ran on tax cuts. But his economic policies have driven up taxes and costs for all but the wealthiest 1% of Americans, a think tank reports.
articles.body:
The Trump administration's economic policies have driven up taxes and costs for all but the wealthiest 1% of Americans, according to a new analysis from an economic think tank.

A typical American consumer, someone in the middle 20% by income, will pay about $1,700 more in taxes and other costs in 2026 because of Trump's policies, the report found. The poorest 20% will pay about $750 more.

Only the top 1% of earners will pay less: $12,560 less, according to the report from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP), a left-leaning think tank.

The Oct. 8 release focuses on three major policy changes under the second Trump administration: new tax provisions enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the expiration of Affordable Care Act tax credits from the COVID-19 era, and price increases triggered by tariffs, the Iran war and immigration actions.

Those added costs may help explain why consumer confidence stands near an all-time low , and why household debt is rising , at a time when the U.S. economy appears strong on other measures.

"No matter how much the Trump administration touts the tax cuts that they've enacted, they can't get around the fact that they've caused increased costs that more than offset those tax cuts by a lot for most people, except for the rich," said Steve Wamhoff , federal tax policy director at ITEP.

Did Trump's economic policies raise costs for Americans?

The report comes from a group that is generally critical of the Trump administration and its economic policies.

In response, the Trump administration offered a very different assessment of the president's impact on the U.S. economy.

" President Trump 's aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda has stopped [former President Joe] Biden's inflation crisis, driven economic growth, and created private-sector jobs, and will continue to deliver economic wins over the next two years," said White House spokesman Matthew Middleton.

Middleton added, "Democrats pretend to care about 'affordability' while supporting socialist candidates whose policies would cost every American household $355,000 over 10 years while adding $49 trillion to the deficit."

A White House report on the Trump tax cuts, released in June, found that they "delivered the largest share of tax relief directly to millions of low- and middle- income Americans."

Other policy experts questioned some findings in the ITEP report. A lot depends on how you score Trump's policy moves.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act extended tax cuts Congress approved during the first Trump administration under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, along with some new cuts.

articles.title: Republicans warn that Pentagon funds will hinge on Trump getting tougher with Russia
articles.summary: A growing chorus of House Republicans is warning President Trump that they’re ready to block additional Pentagon funding unless the administration gets tougher on Russia. Behind Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the administration is pushing Republicans on Capitol Hill to approve at least $350 billion in new military spending as part of a partisan reconciliation package…
articles.body:
A growing chorus of House Republicans is warning President Trump that they’re ready to block additional Pentagon funding unless the administration gets tougher on Russia.

Behind Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the administration is pushing Republicans on Capitol Hill to approve at least $350 billion in new military spending as part of a partisan reconciliation package in the postelection lame-duck session.

But several of Ukraine’s GOP allies are furious with Trump’s latest foreign policy moves, chief among them a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel to America in an effort to curb rising fuel costs.

That agreement, combined with reports that the U.S. has restricted Ukraine’s use of strategic satellite systems, has set the stage for a pitched internal fight in the lame-duck session, pitting Kyiv’s staunchest Republican allies — who want the Russian sanctions restored and the satellite limits removed — against the administration as it races to secure the boost in Pentagon funds.

Fueling that clash is legislation , sponsored by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) and signed by Trump just last month, which was designed to tighten sanctions on Russia and put additional pressure on Moscow to reach a peace deal with Ukraine. Trump’s move to waive those sanctions instead has boosted Putin’s ability to fund the war, frustrating the bill’s supporters in both parties.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) warned this week that no part of Trump’s legislative agenda will pass through Congress in the lame-duck session unless Trump takes steps to punish the Russian war machine, rather than feeding it. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) told The Wall Street Journal that there will be “consequences” if the administration doesn’t take steps to restore the satellite technologies that Ukraine says have been restricted.

“Agencies won’t get funding if they’re not doing their jobs,” Fitzpatrick said.

And other Republicans on Capitol Hill say those warnings have teeth, not only because of the anger Trump’s decisions have stirred, but also because many Republicans won’t be back in Congress next year — either due to retirement or defeat — which will liberate them to vote against the president without fear of a political backlash.

“There’s going to be enough pressure from the Hill that the admin recognizes that they need to back off, to some degree, if they actually want to get something done,” a House GOP aide said. “There are enough members who are either not returning, or who are going to — after the elections who [have] lost — who are going to feel, maybe, unshackled from their responsibility to be in lock step with the president.”

The Pentagon chief for months has pushed Congress to authorize Trump’s record $1.5 trillion defense budget request, dubbing it a “one-time generational investment” paramount to achieving Trump’s national security priorities.

And the Defense secretary said this past week the Pentagon will forcefully push for the $350 billion reconciliation package, which remains stalled on Capitol Hill over differences on how to fund it.

“We’re running fast immediately with the committees to ensure that that reconciliation bill, at a minimum of $350 [billion], potentially more, ultimately fills up what this department needs in order for the president to ensure that we reestablish deterrence and rebuild the military around the world,” Hegseth said Wednesday at an Army conference in Washington, D.C., noting the Pentagon is working with the White House to make it happen “regardless” of the midterm results.

The package includes funds for several of Trump’s priorities, including $17 billion for the Golden Dome homeland missile defense system, drones and $47 billion for expanded munitions production.

Of the $113 billion designated to boost the defense industrial base, more than $48 billion is for critical minerals. About $103 billion is set for low-cost autonomous systems, artificial intelligence and counterunmanned systems. Some $14 billion would go toward modernization, sustainment and production of F-35 fighter jets, Boeing B-52 Stratofortress strategic bombers, the next generation of the Navy’s fighter plane and Lockheed Martin KC-130J transport aircraft.

The Pentagon is also asking for $36 billion for a “Warrior Ethos” category that would include investments in housing and facilities for service members.

With Democrats near-united in opposition to Trump’s Iran war, GOP leaders will need virtually every House Republican to support the package to have any chance of moving through the lower chamber.

But Bacon, who’s retiring at the end of the term, predicted that Trump’s soft-glove approach to Russia has alienated enough Republicans that Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) will struggle to pass not only the Pentagon funding, but everything else GOP leaders are hoping to pass in the lame-duck session.

“The Administration’s decision to reduce intel sharing to Ukraine & access to Starlink equates to aiding the invader & the war criminal who bombs cities,” Bacon, who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, wrote on the social platform X . “Does the Administration think it will get ANY support for the remainder of the 119th Congress? Their agenda is dead unless they change paths.”

The diesel deal is getting even more blowback.

In a letter to Trump last week, a group of bipartisan lawmakers denounced the agreement , suggesting it violated the spirit, if not the letter, of the new Russian sanctions law. They urged the president to reverse course by installing the law’s sanctions “to their fullest extent and without delay.”

“We urge the Administration to revoke this license and not issue further general licenses that reopen Russian energy transactions and restore revenue to the Kremlin’s war chest,” the lawmakers wrote.

Five Republicans endorsed the letter: Reps. Michael McCaul (Texas), Dan Newhouse (Wash.) and Joe Wilson (S.C.) along with Bacon and Fitzpatrick.

Wilson, a co-chair of the House Ukraine Caucus, issued a subsequent statement that gave Trump another nudge by pointing out that the president had championed the brand new sanctions bill.

“President Trump supported these robust sanctions championed by the late Senator Graham,” Wilson said. “I believe implementation of the Graham sanctions passed by Congress and signed by President Trump remains critical to advancing American interests.”

Other Republicans, speaking anonymously, were much more forceful, even placing the blame for the diesel cost crisis on Trump for launching the Iran war.

“He needs to drop this decision,” the House GOP aide said.

“Like, A, it’s illegal. We passed a law saying there’s an energy ban on Russia,” the aide continued. “But at the same time, why did we get ourselves into a war in the Middle East to upset fuel prices? You want to lower fuel prices, figure that out.”

To quell the skepticism over the Trump administration’s defense spending plans, the Pentagon officials recently embarked on a series of closed-door briefings to carve out a lane for the $1.5 trillion budget request.

But Democrats and some Senate Republicans worry the late-stage barrage of classified sessions so close to the end of the year won’t yield the necessary coalition of lawmakers to move the needle.

articles.title: Maybe There Was an Egg Cartel After All
articles.summary: For years, economists dismissed collusion as crankery and blamed bird flu for high prices. Then the feds found evidence that could prove the cranks right, an...
articles.body:
When you see the cost of an everyday item — the kind you're going to buy regardless of price — more than double in a year, do you get suspicious?

When it came to eggs, whose average price in a U.S. supermarket went from $1.93 per dozen in January 2022 to $4.82 a year later — and not even for the lovingly cared-for, cage-free variety — Americans had their choice of explanations. Some supply chain experts pointed to continued pandemic-era disruptions. The geopolitically minded cited impacts of war in agriculturally productive Ukraine, shrinking global supply while driving up fuel and feed costs. Republicans blamed the Democratic administration for wild spending that prompted widespread "Bidenflation." Most Americans appeared content with the prevailing rationale they were given: Bird flu, an epidemic with a near-100% mortality rate, contributed to the death of 43 million egg-laying hens in 2022 alone while consumers continued to crave omelettes.

Peter Carstensen, a law school professor and fellow at the American Antitrust Institute, watched the prices of eggs rise from his Wisconsin home and suspected all those explanations were ignoring the potential for human villainy in a market where demand remains fixed. "Eggs are a classic example of where collusion makes an awful lot of sense," said Carstensen. "I am going to have my two eggs and bacon every Wednesday, and on Saturday as well, regardless of the price of eggs."

The suspicion of antitrust hawks like Carstensen — that producers were choosing to raise prices in tandem to increase profits rather than competing in a way that would drive prices down — was dismissed by mainstream economists and commentators as the work of cranks looking past simple economics for a true crime story that could exist only in their minds. Washington Post columnist Megan McArdle waved away "internet memes and a fair amount of conspiracizing," as she put it, "about monopolistic egg producers colluding to raid the pockets of hard-working, egg-loving Americans."

Other free marketeers made it a Rorschach test of financial literacy flunked by those desperate to feed a populist cause. "You don't need shadowy conspiracies of egg producers to understand the dynamics of egg-flation in the United States," agricultural economist Jeremy Horpedahl wrote on a blog for the libertarian Cato Institute. "All you need to explain the price fluctuations of eggs is good old supply and demand."

The truth was out there. Investigators found what they considered evidence of a scheme in which three of the country's largest egg producers coordinated inflated bids to a central price clearinghouse so as to artificially drive up prices in ways immediately felt by consumers, as the U.S. Justice Department and 17 state attorneys general outlined in a lawsuit. It took three years for them to disentangle the alleged conspiracy, with limited consequences for the companies, which never admitted wrongdoing. The cranks, it turned out, just saw what no one else did — and the rest of us are still catching up.

articles.title: ‘You Barely Understand Regular Money’: Why Young Men Keep Gambling
articles.summary: Politics isn't ready for the rise of easy-access gambling platforms.
articles.body:
If $10,000 can't buy you a house, why not gamble it?

That might not seem like a sound financial decision, but it's an increasingly familiar mindset for many Americans — particularly young men — who are watching prices march steadily higher and feeling like they can't keep up.

Jonathan Cohen, gambling policy lead at the American Institute for Boys and Men, told me inflation in general and the unaffordability of housing in particular has fed a rise in financial nihilism and pushed many people to look for easy ways to ramp up their bank balances.

"With a couple of Eagles parlays, I have a chance of making [that $10,000] into $100,000," he said. "Now I have a down payment."

Gambling, meme stocks, crypto and other get-rich-quick schemes have soared in popularity alongside inflation, fed by a much more permissive regulatory environment for such products in the past few years. And research supports the theory that a lot of people think of gambling as a way to build wealth, or at least as similar to investing: A paper published last month shows that, when states legalize gambling, the money households put into wagers displaces investment activity, rather than purchases.

At the same time, data from the Citizens Capital Markets and Advisory investment bank shows that the median users of sports gambling apps and prediction markets lose money on net.

Obviously, risky bets have grown in popularity in part because betting is fun. But Washington bears responsibility too: Economic and political realities shaped by decisions here seem to be greasing the skids for potentially destructive financial behaviors.

Ethan Simmons-Patterson, a 33-year-old standup comedian and pediatric nurse who lives in Brooklyn, told me he's been troubled by what he hears from his friends and other young men, like the early-20s guys he plays basketball with at the YMCA.

"'If I get in crypto, I get invested. I can make money,'" they say, according to Simmons-Patterson. "'The president has a coin. The president's hustling.'"

"I watched my friends talk about it in a way that they thought they had struck gold, or struck oil or something like that," he added. "And in my mind, I'm looking at these guys like, 'You barely understand regular money.'"

He also described the ubiquitous culture of sports gambling.

"They talk about how much money they're losing," he said. "And they're getting into obscure sports like women's college volleyball, stuff they've never watched, just so they could gamble."

articles.title: Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
articles.summary: Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on autonomous vehicles, policy, and road rules, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started The first state to pass a law legalizing self-driving cars operating on public roads was Nevada in June 2011 — long before such vehicles were operating on public roads. This was three years before the introduction of Tesla’s Autopilot, five years before Waymo spun out of the Google self-driving car project, and seven years before the first commercial robotaxi service got underway (in Arizona, not Nevada). Nevada was ahead of the curve primarily due to lobbying: Google saw Nevada as prime testing ground for its prototypes, so it urged lawmakers to pass the law that allowed it to do so. The legislation even included a provision exempting drivers from text-messaging bans while the automated system was engaged. Back then, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars with open arms, eager to be seen as future-forward and pro-innovation. They had no inkling that over a decade later, they would be back at the drafting table crafting legislation to rein in these same self-driving cars. While federal regulators scramble to establish safety standards, legislation that would establish rules for autonomous vehicles remains stalled in Congress — and has been for years. Washington’s paralysis has left local lawmakers to create their own playbooks to ensure robot cars at least follow some rules of the road. The result is a patchwork of rules and regulations for robotaxi operators to follow — an outcome that many industry leaders were desperate to avoid. And as robotaxis continue to spread to new cities, local officials are discovering more unintended consequences of their new robot residents, leading to even more rules and an ever-growing patchwork of complexity for operators. How it’s going Municipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, but they hold broad authority over street operations. As such, they’ve been using that authority to pass their own laws governing the rollout of robotaxis. There’s not an exact count of the number of local regulations and ordinances that have been passed since robotaxis have gone mainstream. But in the absence of any federal rules, cities and states have been flexing their authority in an effort to bring order to some of the chaos. Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies direct control over AVs in emergencies. And Austin firefighters have expressed concern over the Tesla Cybercab’s lack of steering wheel or pedals, which they argue could lead to issues if first responders need to move a stalled vehicle. They want to require AV developers to establish dedicated, rapid-response towing protocols and direct human operator communications for emergency situations. It’s not just cities or blue states taking a harder line, either — the pushback is blurring traditional political lines. It used to be the case that Republicans were seen as more welcoming of autonomous vehicles, while Democrats were seen as more skeptical. This has certainly borne out in a handful of Democrat-led cities — New York City, Chicago, Washington, DC — that still haven’t legalized driverless cars. But now even some red states are considering tightening the leash, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Iowa. Even in tech-friendly California, state lawmakers are mulling ways to bring robotaxis to heel. Several bills have been introduced to give cities direct authority to limit AV fleet sizes, restrict operating hours, or enact local permit bans within municipal limits. Additionally, emergency protocols were drafted to require AV companies to give local police and fire departments physical override access or emergency remote shut-off mechanisms. Some municipalities are flexing their land-use and zoning powers to crack down on robot cars. Culver City explored emergency moratoriums on building permits for AV fleet facilities, while Santa Monica used local noise and traffic ordinances to restrict 24-hour charging hubs. It would seem that even robotaxis aren’t immune to NIMBY complaints. What happens next As the local debate over autonomous vehicles intensifies, AV developers are increasingly looking overseas as a potential hedge to more obstacles in cropping up in the US. Waymo is planning to expand its service in London, Tokyo, and Munich. Uber is teeing up vehicles for Manchester, Madrid, and Dubai. If the US is getting too complex and over-regulated, perhaps they can find friendlier reception elsewhere. Still, the US presents the industry’s best chances of turning a profit, especially as costs for developers continue to grow. Rather than fighting strict local regulations head-on, companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Aurora are prioritizing states with explicit legislative preemption that prevents individual cities from banning the technology. And at the national level, industry trade groups like the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association are aggressively pushing for more preemption powers in an attempt to create more unified standards. Congress may eventually get around to passing high-level safety legislation, but it’s highly unlikely that any bill passed at the federal level would seek to strip cities of their core police, zoning, and emergency response powers. States will also have a say, and sometimes that may complement or conflict with their own cities. Even airport authorities are getting in on the action, proposing their own slate of rules for robotaxis. AV companies would be well advised to get used to the patchwork — it’s not going anywhere. By the way * Even if the feds pass a sweeping national framework, like the proposed SELF DRIVE Act, cities and states would still keep their authority over local road usage. In other words, cities are going to be the main arbiters of robotaxi permission for the foreseeable future. * Texas may be the Wild West, with fewer rules governing self-driving cars than most states, but California is still the gold standard. Securing a deployment permit from the California Public Utilities Commission, for example, is viewed by the industry as a definitive safety validation. Read this * Streetsblog reports that Uber and Waymo have spent more than $15 million on lobbying state officials in New York. * Tesla had to change the name of its Full Self-Driving software to “Assisted Driving” to win approval from European Union regulators, Reuters reports. * Tesla provided first responders in Austin three days of training and emergency guidebooks on how to interact with its Cybercabs, according to The Daily Texan.

articles.title: Trump’s Latin America Allies Deepen Ties With Washington Lenders
articles.summary: Latin America’s rightward, market-friendly shift is reshaping its relationship with Donald Trump’s Washington, including new flows of money from the multilat...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Latin America's rightward, market-friendly shift is reshaping its relationship with Donald Trump's Washington, including new flows of money from the multilateral lenders historically villainized in the region for pushing fiscal austerity.

The alignment was on full display at the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok over the past week, as officials from the so-called Bretton Woods institutions embraced many of the policies being pursued by new, Trump-aligned governments. They also described growing demand across the region for fresh funding and policy guidance.

"We do see a shift in policy direction," Nigel Chalk, director of the IMF's Western Hemisphere Department, said at a briefing Friday. "We see our role as supporting that shift toward more socially conscious, more fiscally responsible, more market-oriented policies in the region."

The growing footprint coincides with a dramatic redrawing of Latin America's political map, including leaders aligned more closely with Trump.

The IMF has 10 active programs in the Americas, according to Chalk, out of a total of 35 active lending programs. That includes a precautionary line with Chile and fresh financing for Bolivia, as well as active talks with Colombia for a new program — all of which recently elected Trump-backed presidents. It's also active in MAGA-inspired El Salvador and Argentina, while both the fund and the bank are reenaged with Washington-controlled Venezuela.

To be sure, Chalk and and his counterpart at the World Bank, Susana Cordeiro Guerra, said politics doesn't play a role, and kept Trump out of the discussions this week.

"The bank is agnostic, as much as we can, to the politics of reform," Cordeiro Guerra said. The increased engagement with the new leaders is because "the overlap with the jobs and growth agenda is tremendous."

While many world leaders' relationships with Trump are more personal and transactional than ideological, his Republican party has traditionally backed the fiscal discipline and market-friendly policies of the IMF, known as the Washington Consensus, and is more aligned with right-wing parties globally on issues of immigration and security.

articles.title: New rule could impact your next delayed or canceled flight
articles.summary: The next time your flight is canceled or delayed, it may not be as easy to get compensation as a new federal rule takes effect.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – The next time your flight is canceled or delayed, it may not be as easy to get compensation once a new federal rule takes effect.

Last month, the Transportation Department announced that 10 types of flight disruptions would no longer be attributed to the air carrier. Instead, the 10 disruptions, listed below, will be tracked in the new “Section 511(b) category.”

Aircraft cleaning needed after the death of a passenger.

Aircraft damage caused by extreme weather, foreign object debris, or sabotage.

A baggage or cargo loading delay caused by an outage of a bag system not controlled by a carrier or its contractor.

Cybersecurity attacks, as long as the air carrier is in compliance with applicable cybersecurity regulations.

A shutdown or system failure of government systems that directly affects the ability of an air carrier to safely conduct flights and is unexpected.

Overheated brakes due to a safety incident resulting in the use of emergency procedures.

Unscheduled maintenance, including in response to an airworthiness directive, manifesting outside a scheduled maintenance program that cannot be deferred or must be addressed before flight.

An emergency that required medical attention through no fault of the carrier.

An airport closure due to the presence of volcanic ash, wind, or wind shear.

A Transportation Department spokesperson previously told Nexstar the recategorization is in response to the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, which President Biden signed into law over two years ago.

The move, which formally takes effect on Monday, Oct. 19, is meant to “ensure government delay data accurately reflects what airlines can and cannot control.” Airline carriers are expected to save costs by “[reducing] the negative reputational impacts and harm that air carriers currently experience because the attribution of certain delay and cancellation causes to air carriers that this rulemaking addresses as not within their control,” the DOT explained in a federal filing.

Aviation law firm Crowell & Moring LLP called it “a significant step forward for the airline industry,” noting that carriers had argued that the current reporting structure “misattributes certain disruptions to carriers that are not within their operational control.”

It could, however, be “quite a big blow potentially for customers,” Clint Henderson, the managing editor for The Points Guy, told Nexstar last month. The Transportation Department acknowledged that reclassifying the delays and cancellations is expected to reduce “the total value of amenities and compensation currently provided by air carriers to consumers.”

“The one that is especially outrageous to me as a consumer advocate is that if a plane goes mechanical or has maintenance issues, that is no longer considered a reason the airline would give you compensation,” Henderson said. That may mean that, if your flight is canceled for an issue, “the airline wouldn’t necessarily give you food or hotel vouchers.”

Henderson said to be prepared for flight disruptions, “have a backup plan in case things go sideways,” and be aggressive when inquiring about delays and cancellations in order to pursue compensation. That may include asking for a hotel and reimbursement for ride shares, food, and beverages. If an airline declines to offer cash compensation, he suggested asking for miles.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky advised the U.S. that supporting Russian President Vladimir Putin is a “historic mistake.”

“If United States will support Putin, I mean, it’s unbelievable, it’s tragedy, it’s historic mistake and big tragedy. That’s why I think that I don’t want to live in illusions, but I think that we have to be pragmatic,” Zelensky told NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press” in an interview that aired Sunday.

During a Newsmax interview, the president was asked about Ukraine restarting attacks against Russian energy targets following Trump asking Zelensky to halt such strikes.

“Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with,” the president said. “I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country.”

“Well, I think they’re going to if they’re going to end up with a settlement of some kind, they’re not going to do it with [Zelensky],” Trump said when asked if he backed additional military aid for Ukraine.

The president said that he thought the Russia-Ukraine war would “end soon.”

“I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Trump added.

Zelensky also recently slammed the president due to a deal he came to with Russia on diesel, which the Ukrainian leader called a “gift” to Putin. He added that Russia would “‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy.”

articles.title: Infectious disease veterans call for clearer federal message on measles
articles.summary: While money is pumped into state and local health departments to help counter the growing measles outbreaks across the country, experts say clear communication from top health leaders seems lacking and what has been said publicly may have hurt more than helped. The country has surpassed 4,000 measles cases and appears to have already doubled…
articles.body:
While money is pumped into state and local health departments to help counter the growing measles outbreaks across the country, experts say clear communication from top health leaders seems lacking and what has been said publicly may have hurt more than helped.

The country has surpassed 4,000 measles cases and appears to have already doubled the number of measles-related deaths from last year.

Local health departments are simply overwhelmed by the sheer scope of measles cases, according to Adriane Casalotti, chief of government and public affairs for the National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO).

“There’s so much measles out there that the chances of it popping up in different communities is really high. And so, the attention certainly at the local level is very much there,” she said.

In response to the outbreaks, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has issued roughly $100 million in additional funds to state, local and tribal health departments, going toward vaccinations, prevention and disease detection efforts.

This week, the CDC said it would be deploying additional support to Pennsylvania, the state reporting the highest number of cases and the only one with confirmed measles-related deaths.

Despite material and financial support reaching states, what hasn’t flowed as readily from federal authorities is guidance or vocal endorsements of measles vaccinations and mitigation efforts.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz, now two months into the job after the position had long gone unfilled, has had little to say about the ongoing spread of measles. She touched on the outbreak in September during an interview with Atlanta News First (ANF), calling measles “the most contagious disease” and reiterating the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is “safe and effective.”

While officials are commenting on measles outbreaks when asked about them and agencies are continuing to issue support, infectious disease specialists say a strong messaging campaign at the federal level would go a long way toward boosting the measles response.

Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the Infectious Diseases Society of America and former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), opined that an overarching informational message explaining what the MMR vaccine does would be a good start, especially given how many outbreaks there have been this year — 42 at the most recent count.

“I don’t think that pronouncements from the federal government are necessarily going to fill that much more complex space where decisionmaking is impacted by a lot of things we often don’t understand or aren’t articulated,” said Marrazzo.

“I do think that a national message can be crafted to encompass a more broad kind of acceptance of people’s vaccine hesitancy,” she added. “We just haven’t really seen that because, again, I don’t think we’ve seen a full-throated endorsement or explanation of why the vaccine right now is so critical.”

And while experts in the field hold out for stronger messaging from the top, some argue that what has been said publicly may have done more harm to countering the measles spread.

“With an ongoing increase in cases, the standard response is to provide support to jurisdictions, including vaccine, financial resources, and offer staff. These things are currently still happening,” said Demetre Daskalakis, former director of CDC’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases and chief medical officer at Callen-Lorde.

“What is atypical is the friction created by CDC second-guessing Pennsylvania on their adjudication of deaths attributed or related to measles,” he added. “It is also atypical to have a secretary that is a disinformation agent that distorts data to support his personal agenda.”

Daskalakis, who resigned from the CDC last year in protest of what he claimed was overt political interference in the agency’s work, was referring to when federal health leaders, including Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, were quick to question whether the measles deaths in Pennsylvania had really occurred.

The CDC’s total tally of measles deaths does not currently reflect Pennsylvania’s total of six deaths, owing to the CDC switching to a different database for verifying measles deaths and no longer using one in which local jurisdictions can provide real-time case information.

When asked by ANF why CDC isn’t recording these deaths, Schwartz harkened back to the COVID-19 pandemic, when the virus was linked to deaths that may not have been directly caused by it because the individual had tested positive at the time.

“A lot of Americans thought, you know, people are just adding deaths to make this thing look worse than it is. It was a terrible, terrible thing that we had to go through. But definitions matter,” said Schwartz.

Casalotti of NACCHO echoed Daskalakis’s concerns that what has come from the federal level so far hindered anti-measles efforts in some ways.

“When there are mixed messages coming at any of the levels of governmental public health, it makes it a lot harder for the local health departments to do their job,” said Casalotti. “But it also makes it harder for people to figure out ‘What should I be doing?’ when you’re hearing different things.”

Kennedy has a well-known history of questioning the safety and efficacy of the MMR vaccine, famously refusing to discount the possibility it could be linked to autism despite no evidence establishing a connection.

Last year, he called the MMR vaccine the “most effective” way of stopping measles spread and in August said parents should get their children vaccinated against the virus. But at the same time, he has continued to cast doubt on vaccine safety.

“In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said this year at a September conference hosted by Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine group he previously chaired. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.”

He claimed “vaccine-injured children” were “damaged” by conditions like asthma and autism and said sudden infant death syndrome and anorexia were common side effects.

“CDC is also working directly with state and local health departments to provide epidemiological, laboratory, and technical support. Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin have requested CDC Epi-Aid assistance and worked alongside federal teams to help bring their outbreaks rapidly and successfully under control,” HHS senior press secretary Emily Hilliard said in a statement.

“CDC continues to provide guidance and resources to communities responding to outbreaks, and Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles,” Hilliard added.
