articles.title: Oracle Health data breach exposes nearly 20 million patients
articles.summary: The Oracle Health breach exposed medical records, Social Security numbers and diagnoses of nearly 20 million patients across multiple states.
articles.body: When you visit a doctor or hospital, you expect your medical information to stay private. After all, your health records can reveal some of the most personal details about your life. Now, a massive cyberattack involving Oracle Health is raising serious questions about how well that information is protected. Nearly 20 million people reportedly had their personal and medical information compromised in a cyberattack involving older Cerner systems. The attack dates back to early 2025, but new details about its reach are still emerging. For patients, the concern goes well beyond stolen passwords. Hackers may have obtained Social Security numbers, diagnoses and even medical images. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. MEDICAL IDENTITY THEFT FOLLOWS YOU INTO THE DOCTOR'S OFFICE Oracle Health breach reportedly affects nearly 20 million people The Oracle Health data breach appears to be much larger than earlier patient notifications suggested. According to figures reported in filings with the Texas Attorney General, the personal and medical information of approximately 19.9 million people was compromised in a cyberattack involving legacy Cerner systems. The Texas Attorney General's official data breach portal published Cerner's entry on October 2, 2026. It lists 2,992,244 affected Texas residents. The nationwide figure reported in connection with the filing is 19,929,149 people. Oracle has not separately confirmed the nationwide total in a public statement. Still, the reported scale would place this incident among the largest healthcare data breaches in U.S. history. The attack involved older systems belonging to Cerner, an electronic health records company Oracle acquired in June 2022 for approximately $28.3 billion. The business now operates as Oracle Health. Cerner's technology helps hospitals and healthcare providers manage patient information. As a result, unauthorized access to those systems can expose records belonging to patients across multiple healthcare organizations. How hackers broke into Oracle Health's older systems The trouble began in early 2025. Oracle started notifying affected healthcare customers in March after discovering unauthorized access involving older Cerner systems. According to Oracle's customer communications, the company became aware of the incident around February 20, 2025. Investigators found evidence suggesting that an attacker used stolen customer credentials to access a legacy server sometime after January 22. The attacker then copied information to a remote server. The server had not yet been migrated to Oracle Cloud. However, investigators have not publicly established that the server's age caused the breach. The precise way the attacker obtained the stolen credentials also remains unclear. This raises an uncomfortable question. How much sensitive patient information remains on older healthcare systems, even after a major technology company takes ownership? Hackers reportedly demanded millions to keep medical records private The attacker allegedly tried to turn the stolen information into a multimillion-dollar payday. According to earlier BleepingComputer reporting, an individual using the name "Andrew" contacted affected hospitals and demanded cryptocurrency payments. The attacker reportedly threatened to leak or sell stolen patient information unless the victims paid. The individual also allegedly created public websites about the breach to increase pressure on healthcare organizations. At the time, researchers had not established a connection between the attacker and a known ransomware or extortion group. For hospitals, that creates a difficult situation. Even if an organization pays, there is no guarantee the criminal will delete the stolen records or refrain from selling copies. Meanwhile, patients may have no idea their information is being used as leverage. What personal and medical information was stolen? A sample breach notification filed with California regulators provides a closer look at the information potentially exposed. Depending on the patient, the compromised records may have included: The exact information exposed can vary from person to person. However, the combination of personal identifiers and medical details makes this incident particularly troubling. Unlike a stolen credit card, you cannot simply cancel your medical history and request a replacement. Your diagnoses, treatment records and past prescriptions can remain sensitive for years. Criminals could potentially use that information to create convincing medical scams, impersonate patients or commit identity theft. They may also combine medical details with other stolen information to make fraudulent calls and emails appear more credible. FAKE PATIENT PORTAL SCAM CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN AND INFECT YOUR PC Millions of patients affected across multiple states State breach filings offer a clearer view of the attack's scale. The Texas attorney general's October 2, 2026, filing lists 2,992,244 affected residents in Texas alone. Other state notifications show how widely the incident spread. Oregon reported 1,978,661 affected residents, while South Carolina identified 283,903. Washington also reported 69,238 people whose information was compromised. These figures represent portions of the overall incident and should not be added to the nationwide total of nearly 20 million. Meanwhile, filings with Oregon regulators identify January 22 through April 1, 2025, as the reported breach period, with February 20 listed as the discovery date. These disclosures show how complicated healthcare breach reporting can become. Patients in different states may receive notifications at different times, while the full impact can take months or longer to emerge. How the Oracle Health breach compares with other healthcare attacks Unfortunately, healthcare organizations have become attractive targets for cybercriminals. Medical records contain information that can support identity theft and fraud long after an initial attack. One of the biggest examples came in 2024, when attackers targeted Change Healthcare, a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group. That breach ultimately affected approximately 192.7 million people. The Oracle Health incident appears smaller by comparison. Still, a reported 20 million affected individuals represents an enormous amount of sensitive information. The incident also raises questions about how healthcare organizations protect records stored on older systems. Those systems can remain essential to daily operations, even as companies upgrade their technology. In this case, investigators identified stolen credentials as the reported access method, rather than a publicly confirmed vulnerability in the legacy server. We reached out to Oracle Health for comment, but did not hear back before our deadline. How to protect yourself after the Oracle Health data breach You may have never heard of Cerner, even if your hospital uses its technology. That makes it harder to know whether your records were involved. However, there are practical steps you can take now to reduce the risk of identity theft and medical fraud. 1. Watch for a breach notification Check your mail for notices from Cerner, Oracle Health or a healthcare provider you have visited. The notification should explain what information may have been exposed and whether any protective services are available. You can also contact your hospital's privacy office directly. Avoid clicking links in unexpected messages claiming you need to verify your medical records. 2. Freeze your credit if your Social Security number was exposed A credit freeze can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts using your identity. You can request one for free through Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. You'll need to contact all three bureaus separately. A freeze will not prevent every form of identity theft, but it can block an important route criminals use. 3. Check your medical records and insurance statements Review your health insurance explanation of benefits statements for appointments, treatments or prescriptions you do not recognize. Also, look for unfamiliar providers or incorrect information in your medical records. Contact your insurer and healthcare provider if something looks suspicious. Medical identity theft can lead to fraudulent bills and inaccurate patient records, so catching problems early is important. 4. Use strong antivirus software to protect against follow-up scams A healthcare breach can create opportunities for phishing emails and malicious attachments. Strong antivirus software can help detect malware, suspicious downloads and some dangerous links before they cause harm. Keep your devices updated and avoid downloading files from unexpected healthcare messages. Antivirus protection cannot undo the Oracle Health breach, but it can help defend against attacks that follow it. Be alert for convincing medical scams Someone who knows your doctor's name or recent treatment details may sound legitimate over the phone. Criminals could use stolen information to impersonate healthcare workers, demand payments or ask you to confirm your Social Security number. Hang up and call the provider using a number from its official website or your insurance card. Never assume a caller is legitimate simply because they know something about your medical history. 6. Strengthen your account security Use unique passwords for healthcare portals and enable two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever available. A password manager can help you create and store strong passwords without reusing them. If you suspect your account credentials were compromised, change the affected password immediately. Remember, changing a password will not retrieve stolen medical records, but it can help protect your accounts from additional unauthorized access. 7. Consider identity theft protection If your Social Security number was exposed, an identity theft protection service may help you monitor for suspicious activity involving your personal information. Some services also offer alerts and assistance with recovery. Review any free monitoring offered through your breach notification before purchasing a separate plan. Keep in mind that monitoring services cannot guarantee prevention of identity theft or detect every form of medical fraud. You can be extremely careful with your passwords and avoid suspicious links, yet your most sensitive records may still sit on a server you never knew existed. The fact that this attack involved a legacy server makes the situation even more frustrating. Investigators have identified stolen credentials as the reported access method, but we still don't know exactly how those credentials were compromised. When a company acquires a healthcare technology provider, protecting the information already stored in those systems should be a priority. Patients deserve to know that their records remain secure throughout technology upgrades. And consider the timing. The attack dates back to early 2025, yet its potential scale is becoming clearer in October 2026. That's a long time for people to remain uncertain about what happened to their information. Healthcare organizations need to do a better job protecting patient records and communicating clearly when something goes wrong. articles.title: Video game ownership bill introduced in Congress
articles.summary: The Power To The Players Act would guarantee buying a game means you own it, not license it.
articles.body: Rep. Ritchie Torres of New York’s 15th congressional district in the Bronx introduced the Power To The Players Act this week. If passed, the bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to establish regulations that guarantee consumers ownership of a game when they pay for it, rather than a licensing agreement. It’s increasingly common for games sold to require a connection to a server. Meaning that when a company decides to shut down those servers, the games often become unplayable. Rep. Torres singles out NBA 2K25 as a recent example. 2K will be delisting the game from storefronts at the end of the month and shutting down its servers on December 31st, limiting its playability. Concerns around ownership, the ability to play, resell, or transfer games have drawn attention recently following Sony’s announcement that it planned to phase out physical game discs in 2028. In a statement announcing the bill, Rep. Torres said, “A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale.” The bill would not only give players ownership of a game, “rather than a license to play it,” but also require developers to institute an offline mode before shutting down supporting servers. That is similar to the Protect Our Games Act introduced by State Sen. John Kane in Pennsylvania, which would require companies to provide an offline gaming mode, an online gaming mode independent of the company’s servers, or a minimum 25 percent refund when titles are being sunset.

articles.title: Bessent: Zelensky ‘should be careful’ with ‘reckless’ comments that US slowed down Starlink
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky “should be careful” with “reckless” comments about the U.S. slowing down Starlink. “President Trump and Secretary [of State Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that. And I think it is very reckless for President Zelensky to make…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky “should be careful” with “reckless” comments about the U.S. slowing down Starlink.

“President Trump and Secretary [of State Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that. And I think it is very reckless for President Zelensky to make such a charge,” Bessent said on NBC News’s “Meet the Press.”

“How did it get slowed down? How are these disruptions caused? Because President Zelensky also said there was a break in intel sharing as well. Why did that happen?” NBC News’s Kristen Welker pressed Bessent.

“Again, I don’t know anything about that, but we’ve been very clear. And, you know, President Zelensky should be very careful about making statements like this that aren’t true,” Bessent responded.

In an interview with Welker that aired right before her conversation with Bessent, Zelensky told the NBC News anchor that “the message came from” the American government to slow Starlink for Ukraine.

“I don’t know from whom, what cabinet and etcetera. And I think it doesn’t work either way. But I don’t know, really. But we think — it’s not my opinion. It’s opinion of our generals, of our government, and of course my also opinion, the same, that it was a message from American government to limit the speed,” Zelensky said.

On Friday, Trump said that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk caused an outage of Starlink earlier last week.

“I didn’t do that. No, we didn’t do that at all. In fact, I don’t even think it was slowed down from what I understood. Because I just checked this morning,” Trump told reporters Friday.

“I heard about it from the news, the media. And we didn’t slow it down at all. And I think it’s probably functioning, from what I understand,” he continued.

Ukraine reported the outage last Wednesday, with the country claiming its military lost access to the military version of Starlink, which the Eastern European country uses for vital communications.

Starlink services were restricted specifically for objects that travel more than 100 mph, impacting Ukrainian drones, airplanes and helicopters, according to a source familiar with the matter. Some Ukrainian officials suggested the decision to limit its Starlink access may have come from Washington.

articles.title: Wright says Trump administration has not broken promise to lower gas prices amid Iran war
articles.summary: Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sunday said the Trump administration has not broken its promise to lower gas prices as the Iran war stretches into its eighth month. CNN’s Dana Bash asked Wright on “State of the Union” about his predictions early in the conflict that gas prices would decline “within weeks, not months,” and,…
articles.body:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sunday said the Trump administration has not broken its promise to lower gas prices as the Iran war stretches into its eighth month.

CNN’s Dana Bash asked Wright on “State of the Union” about his predictions early in the conflict that gas prices would decline “within weeks, not months,” and, with prices still high, asked if the administration has let Americans down.

“No, we haven’t,” Wright said. “And, Dana, I think you should be –– yes, I think you’re well aware of that. The Iranian government killed 30,000 to 40,000 of their own citizens in January of this year before the conflict. Are you comfortable with a nuclear-armed Iranian regime that’s in power right now? I don’t think anyone is comfortable with that.”

“And when we discussed in March, I said the conflict part, the active war that we were –– the active attacks we were making would be over in four or five or six weeks, and they were,” Wright said. “Gasoline prices did come down. They never got remotely close to $5 a gallon, over $5 a gallon.”

Bash pressed the secretary on whether he is comfortable with where gas prices are, prompting him to reply, “No, of course I’m not comfortable but I’m happy they’re coming down.”

“They have gone down the last few weeks, as have diesel prices, and they will continue to come down. That’s what President Trump works on every day,” he added.

The average cost of gas in the U.S. is $4.29 on Sunday, according to AAA . Last year, the average was $3.04.

But some states have seen gas prices soar over $5 since the Iran war began, notably in the western U.S. The average in the state of Washington is $5.39, $5.40 in Nevada, $5.63 in Hawaii and $6.18 in California, with some gas stations in the Los Angeles area peaking over $7 .

Wright said in May that he was avoiding making predictions on when gas prices would lower, having predicted in March that gas prices would dive below $3 by summer but that there were “no guarantees.” He said the following month that gas prices may not fall below $3 until 2027, which drew criticism from Trump, who called Wright “totally wrong. “

Trump earlier this month announced a diesel deal with Russia that Russia would “immediately” supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global marketplace, with another 500,000 tons coming in November. This was prompted by the rising cost of diesel, which AAA estimates the U.S. average is $6.53.

But the deal drew outcry from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle after approving a sanctions package on Russia amid its war with Ukraine. Some experts say that the release of Russian oil into the marketplace may not lower the cost of diesel in the U.S.

“The announced Russian diesel volumes are a small fraction, less than 5 percent, of U.S. diesel demand over the next few months, so they should have very limited impact on U.S. retail prices,” Isabelle Gilks, principal analyst for retail fuels at Wood Mackenzie, previously told The Hill in a statement.

articles.title: Official data show China is dumping more U.S. Treasury debt. But it may actually be a stealth buyer, with a big stash suspiciously piling up in Canada
articles.summary: Canada's holdings of U.S. Treasuries soared to $465 billion in August from just $169 billion five years ago.
articles.body:
China was once the top holder of U.S. Treasuries but has been shedding its massive stockpile for years, fueling fears of de-dollarization, but official data may not fully capture Beijing's actual portfolio.

The decline began in earnest around 2021, but as recently as April 2022, China still held $1 trillion in Treasury securities. U.S. data on Friday show that's been whittled down to just $591 billion as of August, the lowest in 18 years and down from $700 billion a year earlier.

But the data is collected primarily from U.S.-based custodians and broker-dealers, according to the Treasury Department, which adds that U.S. securities held in overseas custody accounts may not be attributed to the actual owners.

As a result, China watchers have long been skeptical of a wholesale dumping of U.S. assets, pointing to suspicious jumps in Treasury holdings elsewhere that coincide with the steep Chinese drop.

Canada's holdings soared to $465 billion in August from just $169 billion in the same month five years ago . Similarly, Belgium's stockpile shot up to $490.5 billion from $228 billion over the same span. After including other bonds backed by federal housing agencies, the numbers are even more staggering.

To be sure, China has been challenging the U.S. for supremacy in global finance, seeking to unseat the dollar as the world's top currency.

U.S. sanctions against Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine further encouraged the People's Bank of China and other central banks around the world to diversify away from dollar reserves and toward alternative assets like gold.

President Donald Trump's trade war, which has been particularly focused on China, gave Beijing more reasons to ditch Treasuries and decouple from the U.S.

But at the same time, China has relied more heavily on export-led growth in recent years as domestic demand remains stagnant amid the festering property crash and debt hangover.

So despite the friction with the U.S. and other trade partners, China posted a $1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025—the largest in recorded history—growing three times faster than global goods trade.

This year looks to break that record. For the first nine months of 2026, China's trade surplus reached $938 billion , with expectations growing that it could surpass last year's milestone.

Such massive surpluses must be recycled back somewhere, perhaps leading China to shift its Treasury debt to non-U.S. custodian banks in other countries—and not show up as "China" in official U.S. data.

"The evidence that China uses a Canadian custodian for some of its Agencies is especially strong — note the sudden jump in Canada's holdings and the big impact of the detailed June survey at some early points," Brad Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Treasury official, posted on X on Wednesday while highlighting a Bloomberg story on the subject.

articles.title: Trump announces plan for new East Potomac Links golf course
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday announced a plan for a new golf course at East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C. “I am pleased to announce that the Department of the Interior, under the auspices of Secretary Doug Burgum, and in conjunction with famed Golf Course Architect, Tom Fazio, has developed a plan to build a World…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday announced a plan for a new golf course at East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C.

“I am pleased to announce that the Department of the Interior, under the auspices of Secretary Doug Burgum, and in conjunction with famed Golf Course Architect, Tom Fazio, has developed a plan to build a World Class Championship Golf Course on the site of the current East Potomac Golf Links, located in Washington, D.C.,” Trump said in a Sunday morning post on Truth Social.

“When completed, it will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments such as the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and the Presidents Cup,” Trump added.

The president’s post also featured an illustration of the proposed course, with it taking up much of the island that East Potomac Park sits on.

Earlier this week , a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to stop work on the park, the site of the East Potomac Golf Links and a property Trump has been looking at for redevelopment.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes’s order followed hundreds of trees being cut down at the park last weekend. The action appeared to be a violation of a prior order making the Department of the Interior and National Park Service notify the court and preservationist groups suing to halt the project before going further with it.

Reyes’s order restricted tree-cutting and landscaping prior to Oct. 28, with the judge considering a lawsuit accusing the Trump administration of trying to revamp public lands for the president’s own wishes.

In a statement responding to Trump’s Sunday post, Skye Perryman, CEO of Democracy Forward, a group representing the preservationist groups, said, “East Potomac park is a national park, golf course, recreational facility that is meant for everyone to enjoy.”

“Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves and we will continue to work with our plaintiffs to defend it from unlawful and harmful intrusion.”

articles.title: Bessent: Dropping oil prices before 2026 ends ‘will depend’ on Iran conflict
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that oil prices could go down before the end of the year, but it will depend on the Iran war. NBC News’s “Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker asked Bessent about the chances of lower prices by the start of 2027, adding President Trump’s assertion that “this is his…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that oil prices could go down before the end of the year, but it will depend on the Iran war.

NBC News’s “Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker asked Bessent about the chances of lower prices by the start of 2027, adding President Trump’s assertion that “this is his economy.”

“Well, again, it will depend on what happens with the Iran conflict,” Bessent replied.

The secretary said the U.S. was hit with an “energy shock” after the conflict began but that “core inflation is down.”

“The food is below the Fed’s targets,” he continued. “The prescription drugs have had the biggest decrease in history. Rents are down. So this is an energy shock. We will get to the other side of the Iran conflict, and those prices will come down.”

Bessent said wage increases under the Trump administration have stayed “persistent” during the course of the conflict, but Welker said inflation ticked up to 3.7 percent in September after it was at 3 percent when Trump entered office. She asked when the administration will take responsibility for the economy.

“Well, we will own the economy,” Bessent replied. “So far this year, we’ve got a million private-sector jobs. We’ve never had this many people working in the U.S. The net worth of American households are the highest that it’s ever been.”

“So, Kristen, let’s be clear here,” the secretary continued. “This is an energy supply side shock. We will get to the other side of this. This is one factor.”

Trump on Saturday waived Russian sanctions outlined in a recent legislative package named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), days after he struck a deal with the Kremlin to permit diesel fuel into the U.S. and global marketplace, drawing condemnation from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle.

Welker asked Bessent if this deal was “rewarding a dictator who invaded Ukraine.”

“President Trump has made it clear he wants the killing to stop,” he said. “And the so-called Graham bill gives the president the flexibility, gives him 60 days to assess the situation.”

He asked why the U.S. should bear the burden while European countries utilize Russian energy and that the U.S. has not revoked former President Biden’s sanctions on Russia before the transition of power with Trump in January 2025.

A Fox News poll released last week showed 83 percent of Americans are concerned about high gas prices. The price at the pump has soared in the nearly eight months since the Iran war began, with the national average Sunday listed at $4.29, according to AAA .

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that the Trump administration has not broken its promise to lower gas prices, noting they have dropped in recent weeks.

When pressed by CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union” if he was comfortable with the price of gas, Wright replied, “No, of course I’m not comfortable but I’m happy they’re coming down.”

“They have gone down the last few weeks, as have diesel prices, and they will continue to come down. That’s what President Trump works on every day,” he added.

articles.title: Hackers could already be inside American utilities, cyber experts warn of 'Trojan Horse' threat
articles.summary: Cybersecurity experts told Fox News Digital that a cyberattack on French supermarket freezers should warn the U.S. about critical infrastructure gaps.
articles.body: The cyberattack targeting French supermarket freezers and causing millions of dollars in losses last week should be an ominous warning to American businesses, cybersecurity experts told Fox News Digital. Unknown hackers took over the refrigeration in hundreds of supermarkets across France, raising temperatures above 100 degrees Fahrenheit overnight, causing massive spoilage. It could happen here, and it isn't just grocery stores that need to be on guard, John Walsh, senior vice president at the Germany-based software company IGEL, told Fox News Digital. "Think about if we don't have water for seven days, or if they attack freezers and we don't have food," Walsh said. "That's a tough situation for people to live through, and it could create a lot of economic and social unrest. We're seeing that we're vulnerable and that attacks are taking systems down." At IGEL, Walsh works with governments and companies who build and deploy critical infrastructure — such as Siemens and Rockwell — to bolster their operational security. FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE As was the case in France, where Danish commercial refrigeration system manufacturer Danfoss highlighted that many of its affected fridges were legacy systems that no longer receive updates, much of the U.S.’s critical infrastructure is also in need of retooling, Walsh said. "A primary obstacle in [operational technology] environments — whether in food manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, oil, or utilities — is that facilities operate assets that are 15 to 20 years old," Walsh said. "These systems are expensive, fragile, and essential to ongoing operations." FBI OVERHAULS TECH BACKBONE TO COUNTER AI THREATS FROM FOREIGN ADVERSARIES, REDUCE RESPONSE TIMES, PATEL SAYS Decision makers at the companies Walsh works with don’t want to go through the hassle of taking key systems offline in order to upgrade and secure them further, operating under a "if it's not broken, don't fix it" mindset," he said. But critical infrastructure, like almost every aspect of American society, is becoming increasingly integrated with technology and embedded into digital infrastructure, forcing cybersecurity firms to fundamentally shift strategies. BILL GATES SOUNDS ALARM ON AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS, WARNS OF 'NEGATIVE SURPRISES' WITHIN A YEAR "One of the big things we have to consider is that we're moving from a thought process of security to resilience," Walsh said. As AI helps hackers become more sophisticated, it’s no longer wise to attempt to completely shut them out of key systems, Walsh said. System operators are better off assuming the hackers are already there. AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY "Security is kind of like, 'I feel I can trust that things are okay.' Resilience is where you make the assumption the attacker is present—where, when the attacker is present, you control the blast radius," Walsh said. A so-called Trojan horse could already be inside America's electrical grid and other critical infrastructure, just waiting for the adversary to activate it, he said. "They've demonstrated taking it down, which to some degree is them practicing, honing their skills, and honing their methodologies against real targets while sending a message," Walsh said. IRANIAN HACKERS ATTACKED OUR WATER SYSTEMS. HERE ARE 5 THINGS OUR LEADERS NEED TO DO NOW Policy experts are grappling with how to make recommendations to lawmakers, given that so many things we depend on in our everyday lives are connected to the internet. "I am shocked that appliances have access to the internet," Amy Kremer, the chair of Humans First, told Fox News Digital. MAJOR US GROCERY CHAINS HIT BY CYBERSECURITY INCIDENT "I understand the convenience, but at the same time, you are going to have potential problems with it. That should be a concern to all Americans — not just appliances, but things like your Nest thermostat and other devices in your house that could be hacked into," she continued. "As we learn every single day, it's capable of more and more. It's great that we have technology — it's changed the world and made it a much smaller place where we interact and communicate with each other all the time. But with that also comes vulnerabilities," Kremer added. WATER CYBERATTACK HITS AT LEAST 7 STATES America’s critical infrastructure is indeed vulnerable to these types of threats, Walsh said, citing previous examples, including a 2026 coordinated cyberattack on Minnesota’s water systems. "Think about if you were to try to disrupt the U.S. economy or begin to do terrorism-type activities. What would you do? You'd go after water and wastewater. You'd go after the food supply. Exactly what occurred here, but at a larger scale," Walsh said. FIRST ON FOX: TEXAS BECOMES TESTING GROUND FOR NEW DEFENSE AGAINST ATTACKS ON AMERICA’S WATER SYSTEMS "We're definitely more vulnerable, they're definitely targeting us, and citizens, government, and the international community need to get governance in place to push industries to implement these protections," he said. Walsh also warned that this could be just the beginning, claiming a recent string of hacks could be indicative of hackers honing their skill sets as they prepare for bolder attacks. "I do think that what we're beginning to see is a pattern across the U.S., France, and the UK. We see the adversary—potentially a geopolitical adversary—basically practicing their art and demonstrating their art in different locations," he warned. articles.title: A Savannah police officer gave her Flock login to her ICE agent husband
articles.summary: SPD officer Amber Harpe was fired for sharing her Flock access with her ICE agent husband.
articles.body: Now, former Savannah police officer Amber Harpe was fired in August following a department investigation that found she had shared her Flock login information with her husband, Tyler Harpe, an ICE agent. SPD does not share its Flock data with ICE and said sharing access to the system violated the department’s security protocols. While he had unauthorized access to the system, Tyler Harpe conducted 983 searches related to 97 license plates, which were overwhelmingly registered to Hispanic drivers, according to Savannah’s local ABC affiliate, WJCL. The Harpes defended their actions, saying they didn’t use access for personal reasons and that the searches were strictly for “law-enforcement purposes.” Interim Major Max Nowinsky originally recommended a light eight-hour suspension for Harpe. However, Major Michelle Halford and Assistant Police Chief Robert Gavin disagreed, and they removed her from the force. Harpe was fired, along with five other SPD employees, after an internal investigation uncovered Flock misuse. Four of them were later arrested; however, Harpe was not one of them.

articles.title: Carro do deputado do PL preso por disparar arma em balada de SP tinha placa oficial da Alesp que não consta no registro do Poder Legislativo  | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a lei, andar com placa falsa configura o crime de adulteração. A pena é de 3 a 6 anos de prisão, além de multa.
articles.summary: Segundo a lei, andar com placa falsa configura o crime de adulteração. A pena é de 3 a 6 anos de prisão, além de multa.
articles.body:
O deputado estadual Marcelo Aguiar (PL) foi preso ao disparar arma de fogo dentro de uma balada e apresentar sinais de embriaguez. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Preso na madrugada desta segunda-feira (19) por disparar uma arma em uma balada no bairro do Itaim Bibi, na Zona Sul de São Paulo, o deputado estadual Marcelo Aguiar (PL) dirigia um carro com placa da Assembleia Legislativa ( Alesp ) que não está registrado no site do Poder Legislativo paulista.

O site da Alesp mostra que a placa que ele usava em um veículo BYD preto, mas a mesma aparece como registrada em um veículo Corolla Toyota, oficial da casa e pago com dinheiro público.

Em nota, a Alesp informou que “o veículo apontado pela reportagem não faz parte da frota da Assembleia Legislativa de São Paulo e que a Casa acompanhará o caso”.

O site da transparência do Poder Legislativo aponta que a casa tem apenas dois modelos de carro oficiais por contrato: o Corolla Toyota e Fiat FastBack.

Segundo o que o g1 apurou, um deputado estadual pode usar a sua verba de gabinete para alugar um carro fora do contrato da casa. Porém, para usar a placa oficial, ele tem que devolver o carro do contrato oficial e registrar o novo veículo no sistema da assembleia. E o modelo BYD preto em que Marcelo Aguiar usava não consta oficialmente registrado na Alesp (veja aqui).

Segundo o Código Penal Brasileiro, andar com placa falsa (seja de representação do Poder Legislativo ou qualquer outra) configura o crime de adulteração de sinal identificador de veículo. A pena é de reclusão de 3 a 6 anos, além de multa.

Apesar do crime, o boletim de ocorrência do caso não registra oficialmente a descoberta do carro com placa falsa da Assembleia Legislativa.

Carro com placa adulterada usada pelo deputado Marcelo Aguiar (PL) em São Paulo. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

O g1 procurou a Secretaria da Segurança Pública(SSP) para saber o motivo do crime não ter sido registrado no momento que o boletim foi lavrado e aguarda retorno.

A reportagem também procurou o deputado para entender o motivo dele estar com carro com placa adulterada, mas também não recebeu retorno.

Oficialmente, a assessoria de Marcelo Aguiar afirmou que "o parlamentar estava sob efeito de medicamentos fortes, que provocaram uma reação adversa, e acabou se envolvendo em uma discussão".

A equipe dele afirma que, em nenhum momento, o deputado foi preso. Ele apenas prestou esclarecimentos na delegacia e foi liberado em seguida.

"Neste momento, o deputado está em casa e passará por consulta médica. Reitera que confia na Justiça e tem a convicção de que todos os fatos serão devidamente esclarecidos no momento oportuno", afirmou a nota.

Deputado estadual Marcelo Aguiar (PL) é detido em São Paulo após disparar arma acidentalmente em festa, dizem testemunhas — Foto: Reprodução

articles.title: JPMorgan announces $5 billion in investments in companies critical to US national security
articles.summary: By Nupur Anand NEW YORK, Oct 19 (Reuters) - JPMorgan Chase said it has invested $5 billion in equity in industries critical to US economic and national secur...
articles.body:
NEW YORK, Oct 19 (Reuters) - JPMorgan Chase said it has invested $5 billion in equity in industries critical to ‌US economic and national security, as banks seek to ‌capitalize on growing demand for domestic manufacturing, energy infrastructure and supply-chain resilience.

The lender also ​announced it has financed about $230 billion under its Security and Resiliency Initiative since launching the effort a year ago, when it committed to financing $1.5 trillion of US investments in the next decade, including in national security.

Large US ‌banks have already been ⁠investing in rising demand for AI data centers, critical minerals and energy infrastructure upgrades, as President Donald Trump's ⁠administration has prioritized growing US infrastructure to reduce dependence on foreign supply chains in various sectors, including clean energy and rare earths.

JPMorgan said ​its own ​investments have supported companies in sectors ​including advanced manufacturing, energy, supply ‌chains and defense-related technologies.

The bank's equity investments are in venture, growth and later-stage companies, it said, including new investments around next-generation defense technologies, distributed battery storage, automated manufacturing and frontier technologies.

"In the next leg we are going to be focusing on expanding industrial capacity, strengthen supply ‌chains and support the industries that will ​shape long-term economic resilience and national ​security," said Jay Horine, head of ​the security and resiliency initiative at JPMorganChase Global ‌Banking.

Other banks are also working on ​similar initiatives. Bank ​of America in August said it plans to invest $250 billion by July 2027 to support US digital and infrastructure projects.

Morgan Stanley ​has also said it ‌would facilitate roughly $1.5 trillion in investments over the next decade ​for technology and infrastructure projects.

(Reporting by Nupur Anand in ​New York; editing by David Gaffen)

articles.title: Under Trump, deficits remain high while borrowing costs escalate
articles.summary: By Howard Schneider WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - US government debt hit a milestone $40 trillion in August, triggering a potentially uncomfortable debate f...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - US government debt hit a milestone $40 trillion in August, triggering a potentially uncomfortable debate for President Donald Trump and Republicans contesting tight midterm elections next month: whether the world's No. 1 economy is also becoming a riskier credit in financial markets.

World bond markets ‌are driving borrowing costs higher for everyone, and analysts say that the "term premium" – or the return required on a bond tied to the borrower's perceived credit quality – does not ‌seem to show worrisome increases for the United States.

Yet risks remain, analysts say, in part because the Trump administration has not taken concrete steps to reduce US deficits or curb rising borrowing costs, beyond its promise that the US can grow its ​way out of a difficult fiscal predicament.

The administration also says its sweeping trade tariff policy will help ease fiscal pain.

These dynamics are now driving up interest rates for home mortgages and other consumer loans, ahead of the November 3 congressional elections in which polls show Republicans could lose control of the Senate and House of Representatives. Rising costs are the main issue for voters, polls show.

On Friday, the Treasury reported a roughly $2 trillion budget deficit for the fiscal year ended September 30, 12% larger than the previous year's and the biggest since the federal spending surge during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Deficits are usually meant to track ‌the business cycle.

But in the US, they never fully retreated from the ⁠pandemic era because high embedded entitlement payments, tax cuts, increased military spending and, more recently, rising interest costs pressured the government to borrow more.

The fiscal 2026 deficit was the third largest ever, with debt service costs a record $1.36 trillion.

Further, US government spending exceeded receipts by an amount equal to about 6.2% of ⁠the total economy, even as analysts say a sustainable annual deficit, given typical economic growth, is around 3%.

Some of the $40 trillion IOU includes obligations to government entities like the Social Security Trust Fund, while the total owed to Treasury bond holders is around $32 trillion – rivaling the size of the economy.

In another potential risk signal, the debt-to-GDP ratio is now around 100%, a benchmark last seen during the financing of World War ​II.

Economists ​are largely split on whether that is a problem and whether there is a tipping point. They say a ​US debt default, which would shock the global financial system, is highly unlikely.

articles.title: Democrats think cracking down on AI could give them an edge
articles.summary: Democrats are positioning themselves to be a regulatory force over the AI industry should they win back control of Congress in the midterms.
articles.body: Democrats could win back control of Congress this November, and if they do, they’ll need to decide how to approach one of the country’s newest and thorniest political issues: AI. Polls predict Democrats will flip at least one chamber of Congress in the midterm elections, which would put committee leadership back in their hands. That could usher in a wave of newfound scrutiny for AI companies. Top Democrats on key committees have already signaled their willingness to press the industry on tax credits tied to data centers and recent hacking incidents, and would be able to set committee agendas if they take over, allowing them to call CEOs to testify in Congress and demand documents that explain companies’ inner workings. AI issues are already taking a leading role in campaign ads, particularly as data center development has driven residents across the political spectrum to packed local meetings. While President Donald Trump has opposed most regulation of the technology in favor of an accelerationist approach, public opinion polling has shown that Americans have widespread concerns about how AI will impact jobs, education, and other aspects of life. The direction and intensity of that oversight, though, is up for grabs. The issue of AI is “a hundred percent ready for the taking,” says Jesse Lehrich, a Democratic strategist who previously ran a tech accountability advocacy group and worked for Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign. “The question remains open as to whether Democrats are willing and able to seize that opportunity.” AI issues currently include a lot of different things, from monitoring and restricting the development of frontier models to dealing with the effects of job displacement or data centers’ energy demands. Across both parties, lawmakers are still figuring out where to put their stakes in the ground, and early congressional proposals have yet to gain broad consensus. AI caught many lawmakers off guard, says Rob Flaherty, former deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign and a Biden White House alum who cohosts a podcast with Lehrich. “For a long time, Democrats were afraid to talk about it, either for a mix of not understanding it, or being afraid of the money that was going to be poured in by the AI industry,” Flaherty says. But as AI becomes more salient for voters, “there will be immense profit to whoever can speak to the world that we’re moving into at a volume that voters can hear and can feel.” Flaherty recently launched a super PAC called Tomorrow Together with Karthik Ganapathy, a former state communications director for Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign. The group launched its first $4 million ad blitz last week in battleground House races, attacking Republican candidates as out of touch on AI and referencing issues like kids’ online safety and data centers. The group is looking beyond the midterms toward the 2028 presidential election, aiming to hone Democrats’ messaging to double down on what resonates most with voters. While data centers have been the most visible AI issue in many communities, Flaherty says his group’s polling found sweeping bans on state AI regulation — repeatedly pushed by Trump and congressional Republicans — are even more broadly unpopular. Democratic donor and venture capitalist Ron Conway now regrets funding Marc Andreessen-backed pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, Jay Carney, a former Obama press secretary who now runs communications for Conway’s VC fund, told Politico. As of June, LTF spent nearly $45 million over almost a year, with $31 million left in the pot according to Federal Election Commission filings. “At a certain point, voters speak louder than money,” Flaherty says. Even governors who lean toward the center of the Democratic Party, like California’s Gavin Newsom or Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro, have taken bolder stances against AI in recent weeks. Newsom issued an executive order looking to create an AI “kill switch” after previously vetoing a bill that would have instituted some similar measures, and Shapiro reversed course against data centers. Democrats are well positioned to capitalize on the negative sentiment toward AI because Trump’s largely anti-regulation stance has boxed in his party. Though some Republicans, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), have carved out a more skeptical approach to AI, Lehrich says, “I cannot think of a bigger political gift than Donald Trump just wholly bear-hugging the industry and declaring that we must let data reign and any community that rejects data centers is backwards and poor.” A more sweeping AI regulatory agenda might include embedding independent researchers into frontier labs, requiring more safety checks up front, and imposing more liability on tech companies for anything from how their tools affect kids to whether they’re used to discriminate against workers or housing applicants. Lawmakers could also consider ways to meet demands from constituents that AI companies help pay for job displacement and other impacts they’ll have on people’s lives. AI is still not the top issue driving voters to the polls, but Flaherty says that’s not necessarily the right way to think about it. “AI is not an issue as much as it is a story,” he says. “It’s a story of politicians getting bought off by industry. It’s a story of a bunch of guys making you foot the bill for them getting rich while they’re coming to make your life worse. It is a story that fits the national vibe.” Where exactly different policy lines should be drawn on AI is still somewhat unsettled. But Flaherty warns that Democrats risk giving up ground if they fail to take big enough swings. Voters are “giving politicians a lot of leeway to take big swings and to really reimagine stuff,” he says. If politicians only stick to basics like plans to retrain workers at community colleges, “I think we’re going to miss the bigness and the ingenuity that the moment calls for.”

articles.title: Service member who died after rappelling incident at UT San Antonio game identified
articles.summary: The service member who died after falling during a pregame aerial demonstration at a college football game has been identified as Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson, a 15-year military veteran. Patterson was descending on a rope from the rafters during a pregame rappelling demonstration at a University of Texas at San Antonio (UTSA) football game on…
articles.body:
The service member who died after falling during a pregame aerial demonstration at a college football game has been identified as Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson, a 15-year military veteran.

Patterson was descending on a rope from the rafters during a pregame rappelling demonstration at a University of Texas at San Antonio (UTSA) football game on Saturday, where he fell onto the field.

He was taken to a local hospital after the fall and later died from his injuries.

Patterson was a Tactical Air Control Party Instructor from Fort Stewart, Ga. He was assigned to the Air Force’s 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2, according to a statement from the Nellis Air Force Base.

He was one of four service members scheduled to rappel from the rafters as part of UTSA’s annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans game.

“Tech. Sgt. Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing, and to the family, friends, and teammates who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him,” Air Force Brig. Gen. Scott C. Mills, 57th Wing commander, said in a statement. “Our team is now focused on standing beside Ian’s family, loved ones, and fellow Airmen as we navigate this profound loss together.”

Patterns earned several military decorations during his 15 years of service, including the Air and Space Commendation Medal, Army Commendation Medal and Air and Space Achievement Medal. He was also named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the year in 2022.

The incident is currently under investigation.

“We are deeply saddened by the incident that occurred at the start of tonight’s football game,” UTSA said in a statement posted to social media Saturday.

“We recognize that members of our campus community may be emotionally affected by this incident and are activating wellbeing services to support our faculty, staff and students,” the university added.

UTSA football coach Jeff Traylor described the incident as “heartbreaking” and “tragic” while speaking to reporters after the game, according to The Associated Press.

Large-scale deep-sea mining has never been done before, but the seafloor could contain valuable…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is officially moving ahead with a decision to lease ocean tracts off the coast of American Samoa for deep-sea mining.

The decision, announced Monday , would represent the first time the U.S. government has offered up offshore mining leases.

Large-scale deep-sea mining has never been done before, but the seafloor could contain valuable minerals, and the administration is making nearly 32 million acres available for companies to bid on in the hopes of extracting them.

The Trump administration has sought to expand mining both onshore and in the ocean, with the president signing an executive order last year to jump-start the deep-sea mining process.

“Critical minerals are no longer just commodities; they are a vital strategic asset in global competition, essential for reaching our energy efficiency goals, strengthening our national defense, and securing domestic supply chains,” acting Marine Minerals Administration Director Mike Olsen said in a written statement.

The lease sale will be held on Nov. 19. Companies that win bids would be authorized to conduct preliminary activities like mapping but would not be automatically allowed to start mining.

Environmental advocates criticized the move as potentially destructive.

“These lease sales will open the floodgates to the exploitation of our deep seas,” Oceana Defense Campaign Manager Julia Singer said in a written statement.

“Thousands of scientists, local leaders, and community members have warned of the danger that deep-sea mining poses, yet the Trump administration is continuing to ignore widespread opposition to this proposal. The U.S. government should defend the deep, not fast-track its destruction,” Singer added.

American Samoa is a U.S. territory made up of islands in the South Pacific Ocean.

articles.title: Trump creates new women’s health division within NIH
articles.summary: President Trump signed an executive order Monday to bolster federal research surrounding women’s health, crediting first lady Melania Trump for pushing the issue. The order established the Women’s Health Division at the National Institutes of Health and a White House Women’s Health Task Force. The task force will be led by White House chief of…
articles.body:
President Trump signed an executive order Monday to bolster federal research surrounding women’s health, crediting first lady Melania Trump for pushing the issue.

The order established the Women’s Health Division at the National Institutes of Health and a White House Women’s Health Task Force.

The task force will be led by White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Melania Trump, who introduced the order from the White House’s Rose Garden ahead of her husband, said it “establishes a new standard for women’s health in America.”

She said the first task force meeting will take place later Monday.

“Our mission must serve women at every stage of life, from young girls just starting out, to mothers dealing with a complex range of responsibilities, to mature women who deserve to have vitality, dignity and independence,” she said.

The creation of the task force is to ensure that the federal government “pursues a comprehensive approach to women’s health,” a fact sheet from the White House said.

It says that more research is needed in parts of women’s health like Alzheimer’s disease, endometriosis, polyendocrine metabolic ovary syndrome, infertility, maternal health and menopause.

“Today we’re taking historic action to promote women’s health through all phases of life, despite amazing advances in medical science, many diseases and conditions that disproportionately affect women remain chronically understudied,” President Trump said.

The initiative will “promote new research and really go after the understudied diseases affecting women and promote innovative technologies to diagnose conditions sooner and improve treatment using the best available science,” he added.

USA Today reported that the order came after the first lady set up several meetings with physicians and other experts to understand what was needed in women’s health.

articles.body:
The artificial intelligence firm Anthropic announced it will commit 5 percent of its shares to its new public benefit fund as the industry faces heat over its potential impact on society and the labor market.

Anthropic, in a blog post Sunday, said the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will help the company pursue it’s “mission in new ways,” including through large donations to traditional nonprofits or “specific populations.”

The company specifically mentioned AI’s potential impacts on the labor market, writing the technology “may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers.”

“Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed,” the company said, adding the public benefit initiative will “have the versatility to pursue them.”

Stockholders still need to approve the 5 percent commitment, and Anthropic said there is a possibility of setting aside more funds if the company becomes more valuable.

“Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” the Claude-maker wrote.

It comes as Anthropic prepares for its initial public offering (IPO) as soon as next month.

A day later, Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceXAI, said he will give every child in the U.S. next year one SpaceX share.

“This will be the first of many,” Musk wrote in a post on social platform X , which he also owns and is technically part of SpaceX.

SpaceX went public this summer in the biggest IPO on record.

It is not clear how Musk plans to provide shares in the company, though Trump Accounts , the administration’s investment accounts for children, now allow for stock donations.

Musk responded to Anthropic’s announcement on X, saying he recommends “giving the shares directly to the public,” as that is “what I will be doing.”

Venture capitalist David Sacks, President Trump’s former AI and cryptocurrency czar, added, “ Trump Accounts FTW [for the win].”

articles.title: Meta apologizes for suspending ‘No Kings’ Instagram account, blaming bot traffic increase
articles.summary: Facebook’s parent company Meta apologized Sunday for suspending the “No Kings” Instagram account, saying the suspension was caused by a high increase in traffic by bots. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone wrote in a statement that the company’s engineering team found the “spike that triggered the incorrect enforcement was primarily in the account’s ‘reading’ behavior” attributed…
articles.body:
Facebook’s parent company Meta apologized Sunday for suspending the “No Kings” Instagram account, saying the suspension was caused by a high increase in traffic by bots.

Meta spokesperson Andy Stone wrote in a statement that the company’s engineering team found the “spike that triggered the incorrect enforcement was primarily in the account’s ‘reading’ behavior” attributed to the rapid use of the Anthropic model Claude.

“These abrupt, high-volume, sequential requests in a short period resembled automated bot traffic rather than an ordinary human browsing our systems,” he said. “This activity caused our automated protections to incorrectly take the No Kings Instagram account offline. … It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG [Instagram] account.”

Stone explained Saturday that when accounts post, share or comment at high frequencies, they can trigger the platform’s automated systems . He said the activity around Saturday’s demonstration caused the systems to erroneously take action.

“Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error,” Stone said. “Everything is now working as it should, and we sincerely apologize.”

Meta suspended the account for more than an hour, Reuters reported .

The No Kings Coalition, with control of its Instagram account restored, used the platform to blast Meta and say the company “still owes us an explanation.” Organizers said the weekend protests were intended as a “ day of action ” to get Americans to vote early ahead of the midterm elections.

“Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable,” the group wrote . “Meta must answer for this suspension and take immediate steps to ensure it never happens again – to any account, but especially those working to inform voters and encourage participation in our democracy.”

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) questioned the suspension, saying if the traffic increase was real, it was “still a total indictment of Meta’s outsized influence on our culture and politics.”

“How were they not ready for the biggest day of anti-[President] Trump protest of the campaign?” he wrote in a post on the social platform X. “If it wasn’t malevolence, it was likely a natural consequence of a company that is desperate to get as close to Trump as possible (and thus has a disincentive to do the basic, proactive work to be ready to support users on No Kings Day).”

Murphy said the suspension warrants an investigation “to understand why Meta (which effectively functions these days as a private government) was unable to protect protest against Trump, while it spends so much time trying to get close to Trump.”

The No Kings Coalition has led a series of protests aimed at denouncing the president and his administration’s policies since last year. Around 5 million people took to the streets during No Kings marches in June 2025, while 7 million protested the Trump administration last October, organizers said .

articles.title: Judge presses federal government on East Potomac takeover despite Trump attacks
articles.summary: A federal judge on Monday pressed the Trump administration about President Trump’s plan to shut down and renovate East Potomac Park next month despite a previous court order barring any future work at the property while a lawsuit to stop it plays out. Trump in a Truth Social post just minutes before Monday’s hearing…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Monday pressed the Trump administration about President Trump’s plan to shut down and renovate East Potomac Park next month despite a previous court order barring any future work at the property while a lawsuit to stop it plays out.

Trump in a Truth Social post just minutes before Monday’s hearing in Washington court began argued that his administration does not need approval from the court to move ahead with the controversial redevelopment, which includes a total revamp of East Potomac Golf Links and the erasure of miles of walking and biking trails on the island.

The president attacked U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes directly in a separate social media post over the weekend, calling her “insane,” while attorneys for the Department of Justice separately moved for her to recuse herself from presiding over a lawsuit brought by local preservationist groups seeking to halt the work.

Reyes at a hearing last week scolded lawyers for the federal government, which carried out massive tree culling and excavating at the Hains Point location without providing what the judge said was proper notice.

On Monday, she again pressed Department of the Interior officials about their knowledge of plans for the historic site, which Trump said in his social media posts were already in place and set to begin on Nov. 15 when the current golf courses there would be closed.

“There is no universe in which all of this just coincidentally happened at the same time,” Reyes said more than an hour into the proceedings.

Gregory Wischer, the deputy chief of staff for the Department of the Interior, testified that he learned of the “tree management plan” on Oct. 5, and it was part of a slate of D.C. beautification projects being undertaken by the administration.

The lawsuit brought by the D.C. Preservation League and individual golfers, challenges the Trump administration’s plan to overhaul the historic golf courses, which sit on National Park Service land, as unlawful.

East Potomac is used daily by thousands of golfers, bikers and joggers and is seen as a rare affordable option catering to junior and beginner golfers.

Trump’s plans include an 18-hole championship-style facility capable of hosting professional tournaments and designed by leading golf course architect Tom Fazio.

The president over the weekend described current playing conditions at East Potomac as “dangerous” and argued his redevelopment push would inject millions of dollars into the local D.C. community.

Workers removed several hundred trees from the park last weekend as part of what federal officials described as a precursor to restoring the course to its historic design and in line with a 2019 Cultural Landscape Report.

“This plan isn’t just about safety,” Kevin Griess, the superintendent for National Mall and Memorial Parks in the National Park Service (NPS), testified. “It’s about the restoration of the park to its original historic state of a links golf course.”

Asked by Reyes on Monday whether there were any “falling, dangerous and disease-infested trees” remaining on the course, Griess testified that there may have been a “few” prior to last Saturday’s work, but he was unsure about the current situation.

The Justice Department has contended in court filings that the court lacks authority to intervene because the plan has not yet been finalized and does not fall within the scope of “agency action” as defined in the Administrative Procedures Act (APA).

“An agency’s redesign of its facilities does not qualify,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. wrote. “Just as a decision to redesign all the art exhibits in a Smithsonian Museum would not be agency action, neither would a decision to redesign a golf course, or to trim trees, replace fences, expand the fairways, or mow the lawn.”

That filing was signed only by Woodward, and Reyes demanded to know at the outset of the hearing whether any line prosecutors were willing to attach their names. Woodward argued that was “untenable” and inappropriate, but the judge did not relent.

The judge and Abbe Lowell, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, pressed Wischer and Jessica Brown, NPS acting director, on the project’s timeline.

Attorneys for the government repeatedly said they were not aware of impending work planned for the property and argued any such redevelopment would not constitute an official agency action.

“I don’t know what to do when I keep getting different stories from the government,” Reyes, growing frustrated at times, said at one point during Monday’s hearing.

DOJ attorneys asserted attorney-client privilege multiple times during Monday’s testimony, also arguing that officials’ pre-decisional and deliberative communications should be protected from disclosure. Attorneys also sought to shield any communications directly involving Trump on executive privilege grounds.

Reyes said she was “very sensitive” about DOJ’s claims, redirecting the questioning from Lowell at times. She has asked for additional briefings on the issue from both sides.

Late Sunday, Reyes rejected the Justice Department’s demand to disqualify her from the proceedings for violating “basic norms” of fairness, neutrality and impartiality.

The judge called the motion “baseless,” writing in a 13-page order that the government had failed to meet the “demanding legal standard” for recusal.

Reyes is weighing a possible extension to a temporary restraining order barring further work at East Potomac despite Trump’s announced plans.

articles.title: ‘These pilots saved our lives’: Donnie Wahlberg recounts plane skidding off runway, hitting fence
articles.summary: “I’m just going to tell you these pilots saved our lives. And God covered us.”
articles.body:
LAS VEGAS ( KLAS ) – Actor Donnie Wahlberg said he was aboard a plane that skidded off the runway and hit a fence at Las Vegas Harry Reid International Airport over the weekend.

Around 11 a.m. local time Sunday, an aircraft skidded off runway 1L at the airport, making contact with the perimeter fence, the airport said in a social media post . A ground stop was put in place for the airport for several hours.

Wahlberg, who starred in “Boston Blue,” has since revealed he and his team and friends were on that plane.

“I’m OK,” he said in a video posted to Instagram, and seemingly filmed at the airport right after the incident.

“Getting a lot of concerned messages and texts about my [flight’s] failed attempt at leaving Las Vegas this morning,” Wahlberg wrote in the accompanying caption.

In the video, the actor said the plane was preparing to take off but “didn’t get up in the air and ran out of runway.”

“I’m just going to tell you these pilots saved our lives. And God covered us,” he added.

The “New Kids on the Block” member added that the aircraft avoided several fences before ultimately hitting one, but the plane was able to avoid “heavy” airport equipment and vehicles.

In the video, Wahlberg can be seen in front of the plane, which appears to have a wing caught in a fence. On the opposite side is construction equipment and a dumpster. Emergency crews can be seen behind him.

“We just finished praying, and I looked out the window and said, ‘We are not getting up in the air today.’ But we’re safe and thankful and all is well,” he continued.

Wahlberg’s caption on Instagram explained that he originally made the video for his friends and family but decided to share it with the public.

“Thankful to God, of course, and to our incredible pilots who did an amazing job of keeping us safe and avoiding a serious disaster,” he said. “The airplane did take some lumps — but we did not.”

Wahlberg concluded by thanking the emergency personnel on the ground at Harry Reid International, saying they were all “absolutely wonderful.”

The Federal Aviation Administration told People that the plane had eight people on board “when the pilot aborted the takeoff and went off the runway.”

The airport said there were no known injuries caused by the incident. No additional details have been released at this time.

articles.title: FEMA officials weigh changes including less DC ‘centralization’ and ‘realigning’ some staff
articles.summary: The Trump administration is eyeing changes to the structure of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), including less “centralization in Washington, D.C.,” according to two recent memos obtained by The Hill. One, sent out by FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton last week, said the agency “must reduce unnecessary centralization in Washington, D.C. and strengthen the roles…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is eyeing changes to the structure of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), including less “centralization in Washington, D.C.,” according to two recent memos obtained by The Hill.

One, sent out by FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton last week, said the agency “must reduce unnecessary centralization in Washington, D.C. and strengthen the roles of states, regional offices, field leaders and front-line personnel.”

The memo did not say what exactly that would entail. It said FEMA’s regional and field teams, as well as state and local officials, are “well positioned to understand operational conditions … and make timely decisions within established authorities.”

The Hill has reached out to the agency for more information.

More broadly, the memo sought to lay out a strategic direction for the embattled agency, saying it should aim to “reduce federal government dependency,” “deliver America first resilience,” “return power to the American people” and “strengthen national security.”

It comes as the Trump administration has repeatedly indicated that states need to be doing more and the federal government should share less of the cost of preparing for and responding to disasters.

In a separate memo dated Oct. 6 and viewed by The Hill, top FEMA officials suggested “sunsetting” certain FEMA offices and “realigning” others.

It was addressed to Hamilton from Jonathon Myers and David Arnold, both FEMA associate administrators; and Paul Judson, FEMA’s chief financial officer. It’s not clear whether it will ultimately be acted upon.

The memo considered sunsetting offices related to resilience, specifically the resilience-related Office of Business Management, the Office of Resilience Strategy and Resilience Analysis, and the Planning and Information Directorate.

The memo said the agency should “perform a wholesale move and realign all employees from the Office of National Continuity programs” as part of an effort to integrate national security into the agency. It also said FEMA should “realign as necessary” from the Hazard Mitigation Assistance programs in order to support a new mitigation grants division.

The memo further suggested the “consolidation” of the National Flood Insurance Program functions, and it said there is a decision required on whether to “realign employees as necessary” from the Building Resilient Infrastructure Communities branch — a program that helps pay for infrastructure upgrades that help communities prepare for extreme weather. Last year, the Trump administration attempted to shut the program down but was stopped in court.

The Hill has reached out to FEMA for more information on this memo as well.

The disaster response and prevention agency has been in the Trump administration’s crosshairs, with both the president and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem suggesting it be eliminated.

Their rhetoric later shifted away from eliminating the agency wholesale, but officials have still sought to have FEMA pay for less and put states on the hook to cover more costs.

When he was facing confirmation, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that FEMA should be “ restructured, not eliminated .”

Earlier this year, the administration announced formal recommendations for changes at FEMA that included reviewing agency staffing; shifting more responsibility to state, local and tribal authorities; privatizing flood insurance; increasing the threshold for declaring major disasters; and unlocking the additional funding that comes with it.

Meanwhile, agency staffing has dwindled during the Trump administration amid the turmoil at FEMA. In August, the nonpartisan Government Accountability Office said more than 4,300 staffers departed FEMA in fiscal 2025 — more than double the departure rate in fiscal 2024. The office said as of May an additional 2,500 staffers left during fiscal 2026.
